FHA.Nil HAR WELL, JR.
GRAND MASTER
On October 16, 1953, following the unanimous election by his Breth~
ren, Frank Harwell, Jr., was installed as Grand Master of Masons in
California and served with distinction until he surrendered the office to
his successor on October 15, 1954. Brother Harwell was the 88th Grand
Master of the Grand Lodge of California and will rightfully take his
pface with his distinguished predecessors who have served the Grand

~~~.

FRANK HARWELL. JR.
Grand Master
1953-1954

.

Frank Harwell, Jr., was born October 4, 1898, at La Grange, Geor~
gia, son of The Honorable Frank Harwell, member of the judiciary of
the State of Georgia, and Ruth Lovejoy Harwell. True to the tradition
of his parents and his background he was educated in the public schools
of La Grange, later entering the University of Georgia in the Class of
1920. He was a member of Kappa Alpha Fraternity during his years at
the university, which he left to enlist in the United States Infantry, where
he served as a Second Lieutenant in World War I.
Married on March 25, 1925, to Virginia Boston of Marietta, Geor~
gia, the home life of the Harwells has been a happy one for them and a
delightful one for their friends. To them were born three daughtersNancy. Virginia and Patricia-all of whom are now married and two
granddaughter s are the delight of Frank and Virginia Harwell.
Brother Harwell's Masonic career spans only a quarter of a century,
but it has been filled with activity from the time he was raised on April
23, 1929, to the present. He served as Treasurer of Beverly Hills Lodge
No. 528 , in 1930, and became its Master in 1935. His first call to service
in the Grand Lodge was as Inspector in September, 1936, in which ca~
pacity he served until April. 1948, when he was appointed Assistant
Grand Lecturer.
During this same period he served as a Trustee of the Masonic
Homes of California.and as a member of the Special Committee on Masonic Homes Applications and Admissions. He was distinguished as a
ritualist and is perhaps best known in that capacity, but his service to
the Masonic Homes of California was no less outstanding.
His election as Junior Grand Warden in October, 1950, was hailed
by his friends throughout the jurisdiction, as were his successive elec~
tions to Senior Grand Warden in October, 1951. Deputy Grand Master
in October, 1952, and Grand Master in October, 1953, He is a 32°
Mason being a member of the Los Angeles Bodies of the Ancient and
Accepted Scottish Rite.
Upon completion of his service with . the United States forces in
World War I he entered the investment banking business, and his entire

professional life has been in that field. Following his training in the City
of New York he returned to Atlanta, Georgia, removing from there to
Los Angeles in 1927 where he still resides and where he is well known
and highly respected in investment banking circles.
For many years he has been a member of the Board of Vestrymen
of All Saints' Episcopal Church in Beverly Hills and has served with
distinction not only in the activities of his own church but in the diocese
of which it is a member.
After his family and his Lodge, Frank's great loves are golfing, fishing and the outdoors in general. There is no more delightful companion
on a golf course or fishing stream than Frank Harwell, as will be attested
by anyone who has had the good fortune to spend hours with him hitting
a ball or whipping a stream. His clear and true tenor voice has delighted
his locker room companions on more than one occasion and made a
lasting memory of a night around a mountain campfire.
Among his great contributions during his year as Grand Master was
approving and supporting the California Freemason which filled a real
need and was well-received. His courageous handling of the difficult
problem of publications trading on the name of Masonry made possible
the making of long strides in clearing up that perennially bad problem.
Few Grand Masters have travelled farther or given more personal attention to the demands of the office and the needs of the Craft than did
Frank Harwell. Jr., and he will long be remembered for the effective
and devoted service which he rendered.

1, 173 officers and representatives from 604 Chartered Lodges and
fifteen Lodges under dispensation, and 971 Past Masters, and fourteen
distinguished guests from other jurisdictions. were reported as present,
and the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge was opened in ample form, following which the Flag of Our Country was received.
The Grand Master announced the appointment of Assistant Grand
Treasurer, Paul A. Pflueger, to fill the office of Grand Treasurer, and
the appointment of Past Grand Master Arthur M. Warren to serve as
Assistant Grand Treasurer. The Grand Master announced the appointment of Past Grand Master Arthur M. Warren and of Worshipful Leo
E. Anderson to serve on the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
He also announced the appointment of Worshipful Emil W. Trefts and
of Worshipful Robert J. Myers to serve on the Committee on Credentials, and the appointment of Worshipful William F. Jebe to serve on the
Committee on Pay of Members.
All of the above appointments were made by the Grand Master for
this Communication only.

Most Worshipful Sir,
Members of the Grand Lodge of California,
Delegates to the 105th Annual Communication ·
of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge Free
and Accepted M asorts of the State of California
Visiting brethren of distinction,
It is strange that one can have the mingled feelings that I do this
morning standing before this magnificent gathering of men. It is with
a feeling of human inadequacy-it is with a feeling of humility that the
Grand Master should have appointed me to such a distinguished office
in the Grand Lodge, and it is with a feeling of deep gratitude that I have
been privileged to see and experience so much of the fraternal fellowship
of the Masons of this state. I will long cherish these new friendships and
associations.
I have seen the true workings of true Masons-men dedicated to God
and to their fellowmen. These are the ancient landmarks of the craftthe Fatherhood of God, and the Brotherhood of Man.
When a temple is dedicated, the Grand Chaplain prays. "Enable
us to prove to mankind by our actions that our lives are sincerely dedicated to Thee and to the relief and well-being of our fellow creatures."
Again the ancient landmarks. Again the recognition that what is
important is a man's inner life-his spirit. A right relationship to Goda right relationship to one's fellowmen, pre-supposes a right spirit within.
The psalmist, many years ago prayed, "Create in me a clean heart,
0 God; and renew a right spirit within me." Solomon who ordered the
building of the temple at Jerusalem, in the collection of Proverbs, left
for us the words I've chosen for the text:
"The Spirit of Man is the candle of the Lord." ( 20: 27).
And it is about the Spirit of Man that I want to talk this morning.
There is a spirit that I have seen this past year as I've sat in Lodge ·
Rooms in many places-and as I've sat at innumerable dinners before-dinners of Swiss steak, or Roast Beef. or Turkey, or Ham, or Fried
Chicken, or Fish. What we ate was of little importance (except at the

11

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

moment-it was all good, some of it better )-what was important was
the spirit that one felt-a spirit of cordiality, a spirit of enthusiasm, a
spirit of pleasure in a work well done, a spirit of enterprise and of co~
operation and of achievement.
Such a spirit is pleasant to encounter. One senses it--one doesn't
see it. Sometimes in a church building one feels it-he knows there have
been people praying there-that God is real in that place-it is like
something that passes through a congregation-I've felt it in my work
with children as they've prayed for a sick friend--once on a visit to a
camp some of them showed me a field of tall, green wheat-and as I
looked the wind passed over it--one saw its impact on the wheat-and
the children had named it, "The Field Where God Walks."

-I am thinking about the Life of the Spirit in each of us-in any one
of us.

10

And the spirit of a Lodge-the Spirit of a Christian Church or a
Jewish Temple isn't achieved by the magical wave of someone's hand,
or the inspired leadership of a great person-no, it is the sum of the
spirits of many people--our country is great, not because of one, or a
100, or a 1,000 but because of millions who love America-who want
and live and fight and die to keep it free. Men and women and boys and
girls. It is education and freedom, it is opportunity and religion. "One
nation under God" we say. On our currency we stamp and print "In
God We Trust." These are not intended to be empty words-Well~
turned phrases-no they were written because they expressed what the
people of this nation believed. America under God. Liberty, but not
license. Simply put-when one learns to play tennis, or golf, or the
piano, or to swim, or sail a boat-he first learns the laws-he profits by
the experience and wisdom of others-he doesn't throw it all aside and
say "I will play tennis or golf or the piano my way." He applies himself
to master the techniques and the skills of others-he binds himself in
obedience to convention and practice and routine until such obedience
becomes habit. And within that he finds full · expression. And so, too,
with religion-in our Protestant Episcopal Prayer Book we have a
phrase "whose service is perfect freedom" (and in Spanish translation
that phrase has exclamation points before and behind to accentuate its
importance). "One Nation under God"-that means what it sounds like
or we shouldn't say it. If we say it and don't mean it we are indulging
in hypocrisy of the worst sort that almost borders on national treason.
Or so too with the words and forms of Masonic ritual-they are
after all only expressions and symbols of the inner spirit of Masonry--of
men who are Masons. The theological definition of a sacrament is "that
it is an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace."
Many things are sacramental-the handshake of a brother, the American
flag, the Lodge dinner where Masons eat together.
But these expressions of the spirit are in the aggregate-they are the
sum total of the spirit of many. And my message is primarily personal

There are many parts to human life-and there are many ways to
describe it. A man is the total of many things each of them importantone has a body-it is important--one keeps it clean--one protects it and
takes care of it--one eats regularly that it may be strong and function
pt>perly-when it's ill or injured one's living is seriously affected. It is
seen-it can be touched and recognized. It is tangible and obvious.
One also has a mind-in one's youth it is trained in habits and
routines of thinking. It has fed into it in small doses over the years of
one's schooling a vast body of facts that the human race has come to
accept and call education. Most of the activity of this mind takes place
in the brain which is located in our heads. It can be examined in the
operating room. It is tangible and definite. Some of us have learned
to use it well-others not quite so well.
But there is another part to a human being, to a person, that I want
to talk about. We call it the spirit. But this is intangible-we can't see
it or touch it. A surgeon can't examine it on an operating table. But
it's there. And it affects very definitely our bodies and our minds. One
may have a splendid body. and a well trained mind-but if he hasn't also
a good spirit, he is only 2/3 of a person. One can get along with just
a body and a bare minimum of mind and spirit-and most of us know
such creatures on screen or in sports magazines. Or one may have an
extensive edlolcation with a string of degrees and scholastic achievements,
but be completely lacking in a spiritual relationship to God or his fellow~
men, and of such I say he is not truly a complete person. One can get
along, often quite successfully on a partial development-just as a 4
motored plane can limp along with only 3 (or even 2) motors turning.
But it isn't flying at full efficiency or comfort.
And there are many people who limp through life only partially
developed because they have never done anything about their spirits.
They often have happiness, they often have success, perhaps even fame
-but they are not full human beings-not complete persons.
"The Spirit of man is the candle of the Lord." It is in the spirit that
a man has his deepest relationship to Almighty God. The man who is
in touch with the Father is directed by an inner compulsion-by an inner
drive. Words, ceremonies, symbols-are outer expressions of an inner
Reality.
You can't examine the spirit of a man, but you can sense it. Some
people are gracious-some aren't. That's a fine word. It has to do with
mercy, with kindness, with virtue, with courteousness, with sincerity and
naturalness -you can't force yourself to be natural- that would be
unnatural-a contradiction in term.

12

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

One doesn't wake up in the morning and say "Today I will be
happy." and be happy just because he said it. No, happiness is a result
it isn't automatic. So, too, one doesn't say "I will have a good spirit
today." No, the spiritual life also is a result. It isn't automatic. It is
related to the simple things-truth, love, affection, unsel.8shness, honesty,
purity. The mind isn't developed in a day-nor does the body achieve
maturity over night-no, they are both fed-one with knowledge, one
with food. And so too, with the spirit-it must be fed to grow. You
won't get it in a flash, in a moment. It must be trained and nurtured.
1. On our altars is the Great Light of Masonry. It was carried today
in procession by the Grand Bible Bearer. That's fine, it is right to treat
ft with such acclaim, but it is the Great Light not only for the Lodge-and not because it is a venerated volume---:but it is the Great Light for
each of us. We describe it as the rule and guide of our faith. We can
wax eloquent about its sacred pages-but do we read it? (Perhaps such
a question isn't quite fair for the Grand Chaplain to ask.) But this is a
sermon. A sermon is different from an address or a lect:\lre. An address
or lecture presents a subject objectively and generally dispassionate lybut a sermon should disturb--someo ne said it is like a "knock at the
door." As a boy I remember the comic strip, the Katzenjammer Kidsremember them? One of their favorite tricks was to put a burr under the
saddle of the Colonel's horse. And when he jumped into the saddle the
horse ran away. Well, in some such way a sermon should disturb us,
too. Are we feeding our spiritual life by reading God's word.
2. A Mason prays. In the Lodge no important undertaking, no
public function is ever undertaken without invoking the aid of deity.
Is this a form of words devoid of spirit-is it rank hypocrisy? Or is the
Chaplain talking to God? Bringing the Lodge and God into a vital
relationship. Is every one aware of God's Presence there? Is it a two
way relationship from man to God, from God to man?
How many there are in our fraternity who reach out hands of faith
to a Heavenly Father, in sorrow, in trouble and distress and need, who
seek comfort and strength and help and purpose. We live in a world
of problems. In a world filled with pessimism and negative outlookbut such is not for the Mason, the religious man. God is still the God
of the whole earth-of everyone who turns to Him and keeps in touch
with Him. The second disturbing question-Do you pray? Daily?
Once when I was a boy my father let me fish from a row boat tied
to the end of a dock. After awhile I tired of it and pulled on the line
that moored the rowboat to the dock. As I pulled, the dock came over
to me (it seemed to my childish eyes). But of course as I pulled the boat
was drawn to the dock. So with our prayer, not that we pull God over
to us to do what we ask Him, but that we are pulled over to Him. We
don't change His Plan, He changes us!

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

13

3. And thirdly, our fellowship with other religious people. Our
Christian church, our Jewish Temple, the fellowship of believing people.
Are we a part of it? Those who seek to nurture the life of the spirit.
It helps us-we help it. I came into my church the other day alone and
knelt to pray. God was there and very close. And the other day the
church was filled and again I knelt to pray, and God was there and very
close. I need both experiences. I need to pray alone-I need to pray
with other people.
A new darkness threatens to cover the earth, and the candles of
many have burned out. Sure, these are serious day!--lbut God said,
"Let there be Light"-and there was light.
Rufus Jones in New Eyes For Invisibles tells a storyOne of the monks of the desert came to his Abbot one day and said,
"I don't know what is wrong with me, but something is wrong. I keep
all the rules. I fast at all appointed times. I pray according to the pre~
scribed regulations for perfect monks. And yet I am a complete failure.
What is the matter with me?"
The wise old Abbot held up his .8ngers to the sun and showed the
monk the rblood~red light between his .8ngers and said, "You must
become a flame of .Ore."
The spirit of a man can be dwarfed, and puny and crabbed. Or it
can be full and rich and free. "The spirit of a man is the candle of the
Lord." A candle burns-it gives light by burning. We are purified. We
sing a hymn with the words "Thy dross to consume, thy gold to re.One."
It is our spirit God sets on fire. Through us He can give light. Through
us He can show Himself to the world. A candle and light go together.
When we are brought from darkness to light, it is the Great Light of
Masonry we see on the altar. Light guides, it rbeckons, it warms, it gives
security, it attracts, it stabs awake, it shows us the shadows. Every day
a vast body of water is raised in the central ocean many feet above the
surrounding water and held suspended until it breaks on the shores and
makes our tides. It is lifted by the invisible attraction of the moon-all
the wild waters heaving from pole to pole rise obedient to that force.
In all lands. under all skies the invisible power of God lifts human lives
above the level of the surrounding life.
AU life finds its fulfillment in God. Only he truly lives who serves
God in Body, Mind and Spirit. Whatever path or vocation or work he
follows he can find freedom and purpose and peace. When John Oxen~
ham wrote of Jesus of Nazareth he said--and would that I or any of us
could earn the right to it for our EpitaphThis was the life that God had called Him to,
And all that He could give was yet too small;
He gave His rbest, His fullest. noblest best,
and left the rest with God.

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Frank Harwell, Jr.,
Most Worshipful. Right Worshipful, Worshipful Sirs,
And You All My Brethren:
May I first of all bring to You, Most Worshipful Grand Master and
to all your Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California, the greetings
of Most Worshipful Louis Doignon, Grand Maitre de la Grande Loge
de France and thank you for your courtesy to permit me to make the
presentation to Brother Lloyd E. Wilson, your Grand Secretary. While
in Paris last spring, Most Worshipful Grand Master Doignon asked
me to take back to California a medal to present to the Most Worshipful
Lloyd E. Wilson, Past Grand Master and Grand Secretary of the Grand
Lodge Free and Accepted Masons of California.
Before my departure I took the medal and asked Grand Secretary
Charles Riandey to send me credentials and a letter from the Grand
Loge de France for Brother Wilson, who until now was informed only
.unofficially of his being named the first Honorary Member of the Grand
Loge de France, which action took place December 5, 1953.
With your kind permission Most Worshipful Sir, I shall read the
letter of the Grand Loge de France to our dear Brother Grand Secretary.
"Right Worshipful and very dear Brother Wilson:
"The constant attention and your great interest, shown always
towards the Grande Loge de France and to their members. has found
our most lively recognition. On the other hand your important work in
the affairs of .the Grand Lodge of California, with which we are honored to be in fraternal relations and your devotion to the Scottish Rite,
which we practice, have established between us a relationship more than
fraternal.
"The Grande Loge de France had the desire to emphasize those
relations by dedicating to you a medal, to show our appreciation in a
lasting form. Please accept this medal as a token of our true affection.
We would have liked that one of our Grand Officers could have come
to San Francisco to present the medal to you. But that will not be
possible before many months. For that reason we have delegated our
good Brother Felix Lenhart to represent us to you for this occasion. He
knows our sentiment for you and in translating this letter, he will add
the feelings. which are in our heart.
"We hope that one day you will come again to France, and give us
the opportunity of embracing you with our affection.
"Please accept. Right Worshipful and very dear Brother Wilson,
the assurance of our fraternal sentiments.
Pour le Conseil Federal Le Grand Chancelier Charles Riandy."
As you just heard, I am supposed to add some words to the outstanding honor bestowed upon you my dear Brother Lloyd. So let me

to enter legally into this country, a very fine thing indeed to do for one

again he showed his warm heart as a Mason, when he received with

STEVENSON MONUMENT
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Californiia:
WHEREAS, Past Grand Master Jonathan Drake Stevenson, the
first Grand Master of Masons in California and a member of California
Lodge No. 1, F. & A. M ., is buried in an unmarked grave in the common
plot of Laurel Hill Mound Association at Cypress Lawn Cemetery.
Colma, California, and,
WHEREAS, Jonathan Drake Stevenson was a man distinguished
in California history for his contributions to the social and political life
and the economic growth of early California, and,
WHEREAS, he represented California Lodge at the formation of
the Grand Lodge in 1850 and there won the highest acclaim of his fellow
Masons by being elected its first Grand Master, and,
WHEREAS, California Lodge No. 1 has completed arrangements
to reinter the body of this distinguished Mason in its own Lodge Plot
in the same cemetery, and there to erect a fitting monument which will
mark the grave of the first Grand Master of Masons in California, and,
WHEREAS, Deputy Grand Master Henry C. Clausen has consented to dedicate the monument at a ceremony scheduled for November
6, 1954, under the auspices of this Lodge,
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: That the Grand Lodge
of California is respectfully petitioned to defray the cost of providing
a fitting monument over the grave of the late P. G. M. Jonathan D.
Stevenson in the plot of California Lodge at the said Cypress Lawn
Cemetery, in an amount not to exceed $350.00.
Attest:
D. EWING MARSH, Secretary
By Special Resolution of California Lodge No. 1. F. & A. M., at
their Stated Meeting of September 2, 1954-A. L. 5954.
Referred to Committee on Finance.

FUNERAL REVISION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
WHEREAS, the Funeral Service Addendum is not up to date with
the changes of procedure and interpretations of the Funeral Service made
by the·Grand Lodge Ritual Committee: and
WHEREAS, the Master's "committal" in the present Funeral Service ritual is not appropriate when the remains of a Brother are to be
cremated, and the Addendum does not provide any direction or authorization to omit the "committal" in such cases; and
·WHEREAS, parts of the wording of the "committal" (when appropriately given) may be harsh or cold to the widow and friends of the
deceased Brother, particularly the phrases "cold blasts of autumn" and
"chilling blast of death":
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Funeral Service ritual shall pe revised as follows:
That the word "blasts" be deleted from line 8 on page 9 of the Funeral Service and the word "winds" be inserted in its place and stead;
and that the words "the chilling blast of" appearing on lines 15 and 16,
page 9 be deleted; so that the portion of the committal appearing on lines
8 through 20, page 9 shall read as follows: "Though the cold winds of
Autumn may lay them in the dust, and for a time destroy the loveliness
of their existence, yet the destruction is not final. and in the springtime
they shall surely bloom again. So, in the bright morning of the world's
tesurrection, though thy mortal frame be now laid in the dust by Death,
thy spirit shall spring into newness of life and expand in immortal beauty,
in realms beyond the skies. Until then, dear Brother, until then, farewell!"
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the third paragraph of the
Addendum appearing on page 16 commencing with the words "If a
church" and ending with the words "is being offered" be entirely deleted and the following paragraph be inserted in its place and stead:
"The Master, Officers and members wear white aprons, without jewels, and the Master is without a hat or gavel. The family
of the deceased and the Master and minister may decide the order
of the services, if a church or other fraternal service is to be used

in addition to the Masonic service, but the entire Masonic service
must be given. If the Masonic service follows the church or other
fraternal service, the Master as an act of courtesy may request a
participating ordained minister to deliver the final benediction."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the following paragraph be
added to the Addendum on page 18 and immediately preceding the last
paragraph thereof:
"If the remains are to be cremated, the 'committal' should be
omitted and the service concludes with the chaplain's benediction.''
Respectfully submitted,

FLAG CEREMONY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The following amendment to the Monitor and Officers' Manual
would make two changes in the ceremony of Reception of the Flag.
The first change is to make the movements of the deacons correspond to those in the Retirement of the Flag. namely to have the Deacons go to the Altar with the Marshal when he retires. This change
would automatically make the same change in the Reception of Grand
Lodge Officers, since at page 58 of the Monitor it is provided that the
"movements of Marshal and Deacons are same as in Flag ceremony."
The second change is to add what is now actually done in practice,
that is, after placing the Flag in the East, or just before taking it to
retire it, the Marshal places his right hand over his heart.
RESOLVED. that the ceremony of Reception of the Flag ( p. 53 of
Monitor) be amended to read as follows:
After the lodge has been opened, Master says: Brother Marshal,
you will retire and present the Flag of our Country.
Marshal rises, makes sign and goes to the Altar. As Marshal turns
to go to Altar; Deacons rise, take rods, and go to Altar, arriving at the
same time as Marshal. All make sign, about face and walk abreast to
the Tiler's door. Marshal opens door and goes out. Senior Deacon takes
place on north side and Junior Deacon on south side of door, facing
east. Tiler opens door for Marshal on re-entering. (Etc. as in present
ceremony, to the point on page 54, where Marshal places Flag in stand
provided. Then the following: )
Marshal steps back one step. places right hand over heart for an
instant, then drops hand to side; Master puts on hat, and brethren lower
right hands to side. (Etc. to end of present ceremony.)
In the Retirement of Flag (at top of page 55), the ceremony would
read as follows:

ap~lication is referred to it. (Ross Dig .. sec. 225) The proper time for

a favorable report, in which event the balloting upon the application

AMENDMENT OF SECTION 210 OF THE ORDINANCES

WHEREAS, Grand Lodge. Free and Accepted Masons of California and its subordinate lodges, practice the aforementioned doctrines and
teachings by administering relief to distressed Master Masons, their
widows and orphans, and maintain and support Masonic Homes for both
aged Masons and orphans of Masons: and,
WHEREAS, Grand Lodge. Free and Accepted Masons of California, and its subordinate lodges was ruled, on November 18, 1940 and on
July 17, 1944, by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue to 1be exempt
from income tax under Section 101, Subsection ( 3) of the Internal Revenue Code: and,
WHEREAS, under the provisions of Section 23, Subsection ( o) ( 5)
of the Internal Revenue Code, contributions by an individual. during the
taxable year, to or for the use of a domestic fraternal society. order or
association operating under the lodge system, are deductible from income (subject to the present 30% limitation) but only if such contributions or gifts are to be used exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific,
literary or educational purposes, or for the prevention of cruelty to children or animals: and
WHEREAS. it appears that contributions to Grand Lodge, Free and
Accepted Masons of California or to any of its subordinate lodges, or to
any wholly owned and controlled building association thereof, do come
within the purview of Section 23, Subsection ( o) ( 5) of the Internal
Revenue Code, namely, that such contributions are used exclusively in
the furtherance of Masonry in its efforts to promote religion, charity,
education and prevention of cruelty to children:
NOW. THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED: That Grand Lodge,
Free and Accepted Masons of California, take steps at its 105th annual
communication, to be held October 11, 1954 to October 15, 1954, inclusive, to organize or cause to be organized certain charitable Foundation
or Foundations wherein the principal purpose of which, among others,
shall be the owning and operating of Masonic Temples for the use of
such Grand Lodge, and that all surplus funds from the operation thereof by such Foundation or Foundations shall be, from time to time, disbursed and/or donated to the Masonic Homes of California, a non-profit
California corporation.
I HEREBY CERTIFY THAT the foregoing resolution was, upon
motion duly made and seconded, unanimously adopted by Ionic Lodge
No. 520, Free and Accepted Masons of California at its Stated Meeting
on Monday, October 4. 1954.
CLAUDE LENZ, Secretary

PER CAPITA TAX LIMITATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
For the past several years the per capita tax assessed against the
constituent Lodges has gradually increased to an amount which creates
a burden on the Lodges, thereby making it difficult for them to function
free of financial worry, and whereas we do not feel that increasing the
dues at this time is the proper solution, but should be one of restricted
expenditures, we offer the following resolution.
"That the necessary legislation be enacted whereby the Per Capita
Tax assessed the constituent Lodges, by the Grand Lodge, shall not
exceed 20% (twenty per cent) of the minimum dues as established by
the Grand Lodge."
ALLBERT B. CHRISTIANSEN, P. M.

MEMORIAL TEMPLE ASSESSMENT (#2)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
RESOLVED:
1. That an assessment of $4 .00 per year. be, and the same is hereby
levied upon every member of this grand jurisdiction for the term of four
years.
2. That all money from said assessment shall be expended for the
construction of the Masonic Memorial Temple in San Francisco.
3. That each member of this jurisdiction shall pay said assessment
annually at the time he pays his dues, and shall be billed therefor by
the secretary of his Lodge.
4. That any member of this jurisdiction who has heretofore contributed to the fund for building the temple shall, at his option, be given
credit upon said assessment in the amount of his voluntary contribution.
5. That each Lodge in this jurisdiction shall have the power to pay

30

from its general fund, on behalf of any of its members unable so to do,
any part of said assessmt:nt.
6. That each Lodge shall be liable for the full amount of said assessment, proportionate to the membership of such Lodge, in the same manner it is liable for per capita taxes levied by this Grand Lodge.
Poinsettia Lodge No. 633 F. & A. M.
FRED

w. ZANDER

ASSESSMENT OF $10.00 PER MEMBER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
. WHEREAS, in 1953, the Grand Lodge of California took steps
toward building a "California Masonic Memorial Temple" on Nob Hill
in San Francisco, and
WHEREAS, the proposed Temple, when completed, will be a fitting
Memorial to our Masonic War Dead, and will be a credit to every Lodge
in California and to each member thereof. and
WHEREAS. every Lodge in California, in consideration of the
benefits derived from said Temple, should perform its just share of the
labor required to erect that Temple, and
WHEREAS, said Grand Lodge recommended "That our goal be
set at a minimum average contribution from each Lodge, based on the
equivalent of a day's labor, to be not less than an average of $10.00
per member" and
WHEREAS, it has been conclusively proven that said goal is possible of attainment since 45 of the Constituent Lodge have already
reached and exceeded said goal, by voluntary subscriptions, now, therefore
BE IT RESOLVED that the Grand Lodge of California reaffirms
the goal recommended in the 1953 annual Communication, with the
understanding that if said goal is not attained through voluntary subscriptions from the Members, that then, the difference between said
voluntary subscriptions and said goal shall be paid to the California
Masonic Memorial Temple Fund out of the General Fund of said Lodge,
and one-half of said difference shall be so remitted not later than October 1. 1955; and the balance not later than October 1, 1956; and that
the total of said obligation shall be computed on the January 1, 1955
membership roll of each Lodge.
Presented by officers of Live Oak No. 61, Rockridge No. 468, Acorn
No. 494 and Plymouth No. 560.
Referred to Committte on Policy and General Purposes.

COMMITTEE ON RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN
GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The extension of recognition to foreign Grand Lodges is an important and essential function of our Grand Lodge. The subject should
be attended with great care to the end that complete regularity is
assured before amity is accorded. At the present no statutory authority
exists for the appointment of a Committee on Recognition of Foreign
Grand Lodges. Such appointment is at the discretion of the Grand
Master under Sec. 77 of Ross Digest.
It appears that the subject should be dignified by specific statutory
provision:
We therefore present the following:
RESOLVED: That a new section be added to Ross Digest as follows:
Sec. 78.2. A Committee on Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges,
consisting of three members, shall be appointed by the newly installed
Grand Master at each Annual Communication for a term ending at the
close of the next succeeding Annual Communication. It shall be the
duty of said Committee to investigate, consider and report with recommendations direct to Grand Lodge concerning all petitions for recognition by foreign Grand Lodges and matters relating to fraternal intercourse with such Grand Lodges.
Respectfully submitted,
JOHN R. MOORE
CHESTER H. WARLOW
ARTHUR M. WARREN

Again the Assistant Grand Treasurer renders the Annual Report .
for and on •b ehalf of the Grand Treasurer, M. W. Francis V. Keesling.
P. G. M .•. who most unfortunately is still incapacitated. We extend our
best wishes to him.
Detailed financial statements of Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California, the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund and the Masonic Homes
of California are included in the printed Auditor's Reports, to which
reference is hereby made, and which reports are available to all of our
Lodges. Also included therein are complete lists of all securities owned.
These securities are all held in safekeeping by the Trust Department of
the Anglo California National Bank, at its main office in San Francisco.
There is also appended at the end of this report a Consolidated
Statement of Total Assets and Liabilities under the Control of Grand
•
Lodge, as of July 31. 1954.
The Investment Committee of Grand Lodge is composed of the
Grand Treasurer, the Assistant Grand Treasurer, the Chairman of the
Finance Committee, the President of the Masonic Homes Board of
Trustees or a Trustee of that Board designated by him, and the Chairman of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board or a member of that
Board designated by him. The President of the Masonic Homes Board
of Trustees has designated Brother Past Master Ralph H. Head and
the Chairman of the Endowment Board has designated Brother Past
Master Ja'hn W. Davey, as members of the Comm~ttee. With deepest
regret do we give recognition to the sudden passing of P. G. M. Claude
H. Morrison, former Chairman of the Finance Committee, and a highly
valued member of our Investment Committee. P. G. M. Edward H.
Siems was thereupon appointed to the office and is now a member of the
Committee.
Since the adoption of the Prudent Man Rule by Grand Lodge at its
Communication in 1950 the Investment Committee has met regularly
each three months. and between meetings has performed its duties by
mail or telephone. We have now started our fifth year under the Prudent
Man Rule with respect to our investments. By Ordinance, under Section
152.1. the following provisions were established:
GROUP I. At least 40% of the funds available for investment must
be in:
A) Cash and/or bank accounts.
B) Obligations of the United States.
C) Obligations of the State of California and its political
subdivisions.

33

GRANO LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

D) Such other securities as are legal investments for Cali~
fornia savings banks.
GROUP II. Up to 20% may be invested in:
A) Other evidences of indebtedness, which are or will be
fully listed and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities
and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange.
B ) Preferred stocks. which are or will · be fully listed and
registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission as a National Securities Exchange.
Group III. Up to 40% may be invested in:
A) Common stocks, which must be fully listed and registered
on an Exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except that this listing requirement shall not apply to bank and insurance company stocks.
B) Shares of Investment Trusts.
With respect to the authority to invest in Group II and Group III.
the Ordinance reads as follows: "No such investments, however, shall
be made which at the time of purchase will result in the total market
value of the securities referred to in this section exceeding twenty per
cent (or forty per cent) of the total market value of all the cash. bank
accounts and securities held,"-the controlling point being that there
cannot be more than 20% or 40% invested in Groups II and III, respectively. at the time of purchase.
At the Investment Committee meeting on August 12, 1954, it was
decided that the percentages of 40--20-40 for Groups I, II and III be
applied to the total investment portfolio of the combined funds.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Another year has passed swiftly by, and it is again my duty to ren~
der an account of the activities of the Grand Lecturer and the Ritual
Committee since the last Communication of Grand Lodge.
At the end of last year Bro. Augustus H. Allen retired as Assistant
Grand Lecturer for Division Six, a great personal loss to all of the mem~
hers of the Ritual Committee. Grand Lodge is fortunate in being able
to retain his services in another capacity. His successor, Bro. Clark H.
Shaw, comes to the Committee after 43 years of service as an Inspector,
a length of shvice which wiU probably never by equalled.
It was my pleasant duty last Spring to attend all of the Conferences
of Inspectors, conducted by the Assistant Grand Lecturers, as follows:
Division 1 and 2, at Bijou, Lake Tahoe, June 18-20, 1954,
conducted by Worshipful Clare B. Campbell and Worshipful
Ralph M. Foote, jointly.
Division 3, at Guerneville, May 7~9. 1954, conducted by
Worshipful Arthur J. Kahn.
Division 4, at Yosemite Valley, June 11-13, 1954, conducted
by Worshipful Raymond G. Taylor.
Division 5, at Santa Barbara, April 23~25, 1954, conducted
by Worshipful Guy B. Mize.
Division 6, at Del Mar, March 26-28, 1954, conducted by
Worshipful Clark H. Shaw.
At each of these Conferences, the work was fully performed by the
hspectors of the Division in excellent manner. The Grand Master was
present at three of the Conferences, and at three of them the Grand
~cretary spoke to the Inspectors on matters of timely interest. We were
also favored at some of the meetings by the presence of the Deputy

58

59

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Grand Master and Senior Grand Warden. At their Conferences, the
Inspectors of Divisions One, Two, Four and Six had perfect attendance records.
At each of the Conferences, meetings of the Ritual Committee were
held, to consider various matters relating to the uniformity of the work.
A special meeting of the Committee was also held in San Francisco on
November 28th and 29th, 1953, with all members of the Committee present, at which meeting the work of the three degrees and candidates lectures were reviewed and performed.
I am deeply appreciative of the arduous and faithful services of the
brethren who serve you as Assistant Grand Lecturers. I have often expressed my appreciation of the services rendered by the members of
the Inspectoral Corps. I do not think enough praise can be given these
flne brethren.
Reports have been received from all Inspectors in the jurisdiction,
as required by section 53 of the Ordinances. These reports conflrm the
fact that our Lodges generally are in good working condition and that
their officers are maintaining a satisfactory standard of proficiency; and
in those cases where that condition does not prevail, steps are being
taken :by the Inspectors to correct any defects.
Last year, Grand Master Warren requested the Ritual Committe~
to make an interpretation of the funeral service as it pertains to the use
of officers' aprons and jewels. Different practices have prevailed in different localities and lodges. The Committee ruled that while in a lodgeroom service, jewels and officers' aprons were proper and required,
nevertheless for a funeral service outside of the lodgeroom only white
aprons should be worn ·by officers and members alike, without jewels,
and that the Master should use neither hat nor gavel. The written ceremony does not require jewels or officers' aprons. The ruling was made
to secure uniformity and also to eliminate certain incider>ts which have
occurred in the past and have brought criticism on the Craft.
Another matter which came to the Committee's attention during the
year was the use of lantern slides in giving the Master's Lectures in the
flrst and third degrees. The Committee ruled that lantern slides and
other pictorial representations were no part of the lectures as taught in
this jurisdiction, and could not be used in giving of the lectures.
It has been reported to me that there has been a reappearance of
codes or cipher rituals in certain parts of the jurisdiction. I need not
remind the Masters and Wardens-that the use. and even the possession,
of cipher rituals is a violation of our law, and will subject the possessor
to Masonic discipline. (Ross Dig., secs. 502-504.) The Masters should
see to it that these ciphers are eliminated. The Inspectors have been requested to see that the law is enforced.
The Grand Master recently requested the Ritual Committee to rec-

ommend changes in the Monitor and Officers' Manual to make the second order of business at stated meetings, that is, Reports of Investigating ·Committees, conform to the order of business as provided in the
Uniform Code of By-laws, so that the committee reports will be made
under this order of business rather than under the third heading of
"Balloting.'' which follows, or may follow, one type of committee report,
namely a favorable report. A resolution to amend the Monitor in this
respect has been prepared and will be presented.
Your Committee recommends two small changes in the ceremony of
Reception of the Flag. The flrst proposed change is to make the movements of the Deacons correspond to those in the retirement of the Flag,
namely, to have the Deacons go to the altar with the Marshal when he
retires to present the Flag. This will eliminate the straggling of the
Deacons to the door, and in our opinion will add to the dignity of the
ceremony. The second change is to add what is now actually done in
practice, that is, for the Marshal to place his right hand over his heart
after placing the Flag in the East, or just before taking it to retire it.
A resolution to amend the Monitor in this respect has been prepared
and will be presented. Another change which needs no authorization is
the change in the Pledge of Allegiance recently approved by the Congress of the United States, "one nation, under God, indivisible, with
liberty and justice for all."
In closing, may I express my appreciation to the Grand Master for
his many courtesies. and to the Grand Secretary and Assistant Grand
Secretary for, the many helpful things the Grand Lodge office has done
for me and the Ritual Committee throughout the year, and to you, my
brethren. for the privilege of serving you.
Respectfully submitted,
ELBERT

w. DAVIS

Grand Lecturer

MESSAGE OF THE GRAN D MASTE R
FRANK HARWEL L, JR., Grand Master

Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
One year ago you elected me to the office of Grand Master. My
term of office ends with the close of this annual communication. It
now becomes the duty of the Grand Master to present to you "a written
message. therein setting forth all his official acts during the year, exhibiting the general condition of Masonry within the jurisdiction, and recommending such legislation as he may deem necessar y or expedient for the
welfare of the craft."
In complying with this duty, may I first express my appreciation for
the honor you conforre d and for the opportun ity it gave me for service
to our fraternity . They are both great. Unless and until he occupies
this office no man can envision the manifold responsibilities it entails. It
is equally true that he cannot foresee the loyalty, the thoughtf ulness and
the support which he receives from his brethren over the length and
breadth of this large jurisdiction. I am deeply grateful. In presentin g
the account of my stewards hip for your final judgmen t, I tell you in all
sincerity that most of it could not have been accomplished without that
loyal aid. I want each one of you to know, and I wish the record to
show, that I acknowl edge this with heartfelt thanks.
STATE OP THE FRATERN ITY

I am satisfied to report that in my judgmen t the state of the fraternity is of the highest. The Masons I have met and talked with during
the year impress me with their earnest regard for the welfare of the fraternity. They impress me with their concern for the best interests of
the State and Nation. In every community I visited Masons are amon~
the civic leaders, assuming and discharg ing their civic responsibilities .
You may be justly proud of your fraternal relationship.
The reports of the Grand Treasure r and the Grand Secretar y indicate the sound financial condition of your Grand Lodge. With very few
exceptions the same condition exists in the constitue nt Lodges. Several
years ago you amended our Regulations to provide for the investment of
funds of Grand Lodge, the Homes, the Endowm ent Fund, and the
Lodges under a qualified interpret ation of the so-called Prudent Man
Rule. The various financial reports on these funds indicate the wisdom
of that move. We acknowl edge our debt to the members of the Investment Committee of Grand Lodge who have so ably and successfully
directed this vital activity.
The Grand Secretar y's report shows th.a t our membership continues
to increase. There are reasons to believe that the desire of men today to

resulting in steady growth and better attendan ce and lessening the dry
rot which has afflicted us at times.
The Sojourne rs Committee has initiated a program this year which
has aroused the interest of most of our Lodges. The reports of Masters
sent to me show that plans are under way which are causing the Masons
of other jurisdictions, who are permane ntly residing in our midst, to seek
local affiliation and renew the bond of fellowship.
No doubt this has played a part in the unusually large number of
petitions for Dispensa tions to form new Lodges which we have received.
As we begin this communication 17 Lodges are under dispensation. This
indicates a healthy condition, particula rly so because the prelimin ary reports on these groups have shown them to be uniformly composed of

adequate Lodge rooms and provided sound financial structure s. With
the continued growth of population this favorable trend should persist.

The third problem is to find suitable meeting places. One of the most

which are being built in most instances almost entirely with the volunteer labor of the members. They are, indeed. ornamen ts to their cities,

remainder. If this spirit of enterpris e continues to actuate our brethren ,
the problem of halls for our new lodges will be solved.
It has been my good fortune to serve as a Trustee of our Masonic
Homes, off and on, for the last eight years. I can report from firsthand experience that our two Homes are providing for the needs of the
residents in a manner which assures their welfare and comfort. Problems
of staff, admissions, finance, and scores of vexing details are constantfy
before your Board of Trustees who regularly meet in sectional and joint
sessions and devote many hours of unselfish service.
. You may well be proud of your Homes and the support you give
them. The best evidence of your support is the growing Endowm ent

fine motion picture which they jointly produced . It has been most favor-

ably received and has had much to do with increasing the interest in
our Homes and maintaining the steady expansion of the Fund.
A delightful dinner and reception was tendered the Grand Master by
the Directors, staff and students at each of our clubhouses at Berkeley
and Los Angeles. While the enthusiasm of those students participating
is high and the administration is efficient, the situation still leaves much
to be desired. At considerable outlay for initial construction and equip~
ment, and for current operating expense, you have provided these ex~
ceptional clubhouses which are being used to less than 50% of capacity.
I note that previous Grand Masters have expressed similar concern.
Some have suggested means by which a larger student participation
could be encouraged. We are still confronted with the same problem.
Although I confess that I have not found the answer, I have a file of suggestions sent to me, which I am turning over to my successor with the
recommendation that he and the directors try once more to bring about
·a larger use of these excellent facilities.

For the past several years this annual communication has been held
without the presence of Most Worshipful James B. Gist, because of
illness. We were all saddened to learn of his death on April 25. 1954.
Brother Gist was elected and installed Grand Master in October 1933.
He served faithfully and effectively for many years as Trustee of our
Masonic Homes until ill health forced his retirement in 1946. Jim, as he
was familiarly and affectionately known to his many friends, was more
than a brother to your Grand Master. I cannot too highly value his wise
counsel. which was always mine when I needed it, and I pay this personal tribute to a well-loved brother who was like another father.
One of the greatest personal blows to me, and one which I share
with Masons throughout this entire jurisdiction, was suffered in the
death of Most Worshipful William B. Ogden, which occurred in the
early morning hours of September 12, this year.
Brother Ogden had ·been in ill health for the last four years, but his
concern for the affairs of Masonry and his tremendous devotion to duty
never wavered. In my last conversation with him, he expressed the hope
that he would be well enough to attend this communication and discharge
the responsibilities of his position as chairman of the Policy and General
Purposes Committee, on which he had served with distinction since his
year as Grand Master in 1940.
I am sure I may be pardoned for this personal note in telling you
that Bill Ogden was my Inspector when I served in the chairs of my
Lodge. The schooling which I received from this Master of Ritual and
Masonic Law, and many other things not found in books, are lessons
which I shall •not forget. The imprint of his mind and character on
Masonry is deep and his memory is safely recorded in our hearts.
I opened Grand Lodge in Special Communication in Los Angeles on
Wednesday. September 15, 1954, and conducted the last rites for our
beloved brother.
Later in this communication suitable eulogies will be given for these
distinguished servants of Masonry.

GRAND LODGE COMMIITEES AND BOARDS

In reporting to you on the state of the fraternity, reference was made
to the fine work of several committees and boards. I have had occasion
to call on a number of committees for special service, and the response
has been prompt and conclusive. All of this work is going on quietly
behind the scenes. Many of these men are working for you the year
'round, and they are particularly commended.
The chairman of Public Schools Week Committee, George D. Gavin,
submitted to Freedom Foundation ali exhibit of the program for thi£
annual observance. It received the National Award. Our commendation is expressed to the committee. to its chairman, and to those former
members of the committee. all of whom have helped to bring the obser~
vance to this peak of recognition.
NECROLOGY

Your Grand Master had hardly entered upon the duties of his office
when he was shocked to receive word of the death of Most Worshipful
Claude H. Morrison on November 2, 1953. Brother Morrison was
elected and installed Grand Master in October 1943. · His service to
Masonry in that capacity and subsequently as a member and chairman of
the Finance Committee is unsurpassed. The fraternity and his friends
have suffered a great loss. I opened Grand Lodge in Special Communication in San Diego on November 6. 1953, and before a large gathering
of his friends. conducted Masonic services for our departed brother.

year. Several of these are of such importance that I feel they should be
recorded here.
I appointed Most Worshipful Edward H. Siems, Past Grand Mas~
ter, as Chairman of the Finance Committee to fill the vacancy created
by the death of Brother Morrison. We are fortunate that a man of
Brother Siems' ability and experience is available for this important
position.
To take Brother Siems' place on the Policy and General Purposes
CommiUee I appointed Ira W. Coburn, a Past Master of Doric Lodge

On April 30. I boarded the S.S. "Lurline" to make a visit to our
Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands. The succeeding thirty days were filled
with a variety of memorable scenes and events, but none more so than
the inspiring sight of our Masonic emblem flying from the forepeak of
the ship as she steamed out of the harbor.
The hospitality of the people of the Islands is more than a tradition. It is a part of their nature and could not be more sincerely demonstrated than by the manner in which the Grand Master is annually received. Every thought is given to his convenience, comfort and pleasure.
Let me record my deep appreciation.
It seems to be the habit of most of the Grand Masters to attempt
to describe the beauties of the Islands. I shall be satisfied with saying
that I am in sympathy with their feeble and inadequate attempts, because this wonderland of nature beggars description. I could hold no
more pleasant wish than this: That you may be able to go and see for
yottrselves.
I spent approximately half my time visiting the Lodges and our
brethren on the three Islands of Kauai, Maui and Hawaii. In addition
to the official reception by each of the Lodges. it afforded a good opportunity to sound out the individual brethren on many aspects of Masonry
on their particular island and in the islands as a whole.
I pursued the same course in the latter half of my visit, which was
spent on the Island of Oahu, where I was officially received by the five
•
Lodges.
The 'overall position of Masonry in the Islands is good. I found a
deep sense of loyalty and a widespread satisfaction that they are a part
of this jurisdiction.
I cannot close the account of this visit without relating one experience. I was taken aboard the U.S.S. "Arizona", whose battle-scarred
hull rests on the floor of Pearl Harbor. Standing on that section amidship which is above water, and acting in behalf of my brethren, I placed
a beautiful Hawaiian lei at the base of the mast from whose peak "Old
Glory" proudly flies. It was a deeply moving experience and was enhanced as I saw these words inscribed in bronze: "Dedicated to the
eternal memory of our gallant shipmates in the U.S.S. Arizona who
gave their lives in action 7 December, 1941. From today on the U.S.S.
Arizona will again fly our Country's flag just as proudly as she did on
the morning of 7 December, 1941. I am sure the Arizona's crew will
know and appreciate what we are doing. May God make his face to
shine upon them. and grant them peace."
At this point it seems appropriate to make a recommendation. Due
to the exigencies of a global war, flve Grand Masters were deprived of
the opportunity to .visit the Islands. The hand of providence has unfor-

CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE

"This is the Year of the Temple". This slogan has inspired probably
the most widespread and at the same time concentrated endeavor by
our brethren in the history of this jurisdiction. Under the leadership of
Most Woshipful Edward H. Siems, Chairman, together with the mem,b ers of the committee and the administrative staff. this campaign to raise
a building fund has engaged the volunteer efforts of literally thousands
of the brethren who saw within their grasp the realization of all we .
have hoped and planned for.
The report of the committee will tell the story of what you have accomplished. I shall not anticipate it by giving you figures. The total is
not sufficient, in the judgment of myself and the committee, to enable us
to make an outside loan and immediately begin construction. The failure
to reach that goal this year has just one explanation-not enough of the
membership have contributed. The latest report shows that approximately 22,Yi% have participated in the total amount raised.
Regardless of the reasons for this, I know you will join with me in

thanking your committee for their untiring efforts in behalf of this campaign.
And, although we have not yet reached our goal. the showing is by n·o

were obtained in Lodges which put into the field teams of hard workers
who made personal contacts and who would not quit until the job was
done.
More than once in recent months I have said that the Temple will
be built. I believe that you will concur in that statement. There is only
one major unsettled question: When? The answer to that is very simple. When the Masons of California and the Hawaiian Islands provide
the money. The process can be long or short. It is easily within your
power to make it short.
Tomorrow you will listen to the report of your committee. They will
make recommendations. This is your Temple. For seven years you have
said you wanted to build it. I trust that you, as the official representatives
of the 220.000 Masons of this jurisdiction, will have the determination
and enthusiasm to do it now.
PUBLICATIONS

This portion of my message deals with a subject of such vital importance to Masonry and its good name that I wish to very briefly review
past history before taking up the many actions which the disclosure of
facts, heretofore only guessed at, dictated.
In 1951, Grand Master Paulsen appointed a committee to investigate the abuse of so-called Masonic publications and the prevalence of
advertising solicitation by such publications and by Masons of our own
and other jurisdictions. Grand Master Paulsen stated that the report
of that Committee, together with its recommendations, should at least
be a first step toward the solution of this distressing and pressing problem. The special committee on publications reported at length on the
abuses surrounding the publication of so-called Masonic periodicals.
Their conclusion, after many hearings, was that advertising in these
publications appeared to be the major basis of evil to our fraternity and
that many complaints concerning advertising solicitations had come to
their attention. There followed a long list of specific instances of fraud,
high pressure and generally disreputable practice. In clear and unmistakable language, the committee reiterated the stand of Masonry that all
Masons have declared that they were uninfluenced by mercenary motives in seeking admission to our fraternity. that Masonry abhors the
use of its good name for commercial purposes and that advertising practices by so-called Masonic publications had, in numerous instances,
leached the level of a racket which would not be tolerated by this Grand
Lodge.

72

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The resultant legislation amended Section 127 of Ordinances by adding a second paragraph as follows:
"No Lodge or member of a Lodge, without the express sanction of
Grand Lodge, shall solicit, sponsor, insert, place or print advertising of
any kind in or for any medium or publication, which purports to be
Masonic in name or character, or which is published by or for any body,
order or organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership."
Under this legislation, Grand Master Louis C. Drapeau, in 1952,
first set up rules to dean our own house by prohibiting advertising in
Lodge Trestle Boards, rosters, or in programs, circulars, placards, napkins, or similar media: and, secondly, he had forms of application prepared whereby existing commercial publications might obtain sanction
to carry advertising of Masons. These applications specified certain
standards of advertising and ethical business practice which were agreed
to by the publisher and they have governed to this day with no material
change.
The publishers agreed, among other conditions, to the following:
1. That no use would be made of any lodge roster or official membership list.
2. That no money would be accepted from any Lodge for subsciptions or any other purpose whatsoever.
3. That advertising would not be solicited by any person not a
member of a Lodge in this jurisdiction, and never on a commission basis
or by telephone.
4. That no representation would be made that the publication was
representative of Grand Lodge or any constituent Lodge or that any
benefit would accrue to Masonry, directly or indirectly, from its advertising revenues.
Based upon these applications and the promises therein contained,
the following were granted sanction to solicit advertising from Masons:
1. Channel Counties Mason & Eastern Star.
2; San Louis Obispo County Mason and Eastern Star.

These publications can, therefore, be divided into two major categories: ( 1 ) those in which by reason of sanction, Masons might place
advertising, and ( 2) those in which, by reason of either rejection of or
failure to submit applications, Masons might not place advertising.
Your Grand Master was determined that his actions respecting the
problem would be governed neither by passion nor predujice, but by
the facts.
An entirely new committee on publications was named, no member
of which had previously been involved, either in local situations or in
any discussion respecting the problem as a whole. All of the members
had long experience in Grand Lodge affairs, either as Inspectors, Committeemen, or both. The committee was charged to get the facts and to
be guided in its recommendatio ns solely by them.
The report of the committee is background for the actions which I
here report to'you.
As a result of information gathered by the committee, sanction was
withdrawn from the following publications:
1. The Masonic News, Huntington Park, California.
2. Square and Compass, Lomita, California.
3. Seaboard Mason and Eastern Star, Long Beach, California.
4. Southern California Masonic Journal, Ontario, California.
This action was dictated by numerous violations in each case concerning the solicitation of advertising and the violation of the conditions
under which sanction had been granted.
Sanction was also withdrawn from Kern County Masonry and Eastern Star in a separate action. The violation dictating this action involved
the receiving of funds by the publication from each of the Lodges in Kern
County in return for the printing of the Lodge Trestle Board and the
distribution of the magazine to the lodge membership. In further violation, it should be noted, lodge rosters or mailing lists were used by the
publisher in this distribution.
These practices violated, not only the conditions of sanction, but
the decision of Grand Master Drapeau ( Sec. 635a, Ross Digest) dealing

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

specifically with Kern County Masonry and Eastern Star, and the decision of Grand Master Ross ( 732) and the letter of Grand Master
Warren.
A letter was addressed to each Master of the lodges involved, reprimanding him for his part in the practice and directing that it be discontinued immediately.
Lest it be inferred that the publication of joint trestle boards by
lodges of a city or county is to be discouraged, let me say that I most
heartily approve of such joint efforts, provided:
1. The publication remains under the control of the lodges
2. That each lodge contribute its proportionate share of th'e cost
of compiling, printing and mailing.
3. That if concordant or appendant bodies are included, each
such body pay its share (it is unlawful for a lodge to divide its
funds or to subsidize another body).
4. That the lodge roster or mailing list be entrusted only to a bona
fide printer who prints the bulletin or to a bona fide mailing
service, and then for the purpose of mailing only.
I am happy to report to you that most of the Lodges of Kern County
have sought this solution and are now continuing to enjoy news of each
other's activities without the violation of Masonic law. I commend the
Masters for their desire to work out such a solution. Those Lodges not
included are publishing individual Trestleboards.
Numerous requests for sanction, ranging from advertising in cook
books and calendars to the publishing of new magazines purporting to
be Masonic in character were denied. In view of the evidence unearthed
by the Publications Committee, I did not feel that any action should be
taken which would subject this Grand Lodge to an enlargement of the
problem.
A hitherto unused sanction issued to Cecil Loomis, publisher of
Channel Counties Mason, in 1953, for a magazine to be known as "The
Shriner" was revoked when it became known that Brother Loomis was
about to publish this magazine for San Diego Shriners, whereas his
application had set forth, in 1953, the great need of the publication in
Santa Barbara.
The sanction heretofore granted the Masonic Herald, Santa Ana.
was voluntarily surrendered by its publisher and it was accordingly
cancelled.
The Committee, in its investigations of unsanctioned publications,
produced evidence that some members of Lodges of this and other jurisdictions had continued to aid and abet in the extraction of money from
unsuspecting advertisers as donations to Masonry, and to violate our law
in the publishing of periodicals which constitute a fraud upon the public

and a stain upon the good name of Masonry. I have, therefore, directed
that charges of un-Masonic conduct be brought against each of them.
In addition, I directed that charges be preferred against the advertising manager of a previously sanctioned publication for un-Masonic
conduct in the solicitation of advertising while employed by that paper.
I have consulted frequently throughout this year with the Chairman
and the Committee as a whole. The report of the Committee and its
recommendations bear my support. We have amassed the evidence
which will convince each of you that Masonry and the preservation of
its good name are more important than the private gain and profit of a
few individuals.
I trust that you will join with me in thanking the members of this
Committee for their labors. There were few days in the year on which
they were not wrestling with some phase of this problem. They have
done a constructive and comprehensive job. I ask your support in their
conclusions.

"CALIPORNIA FREEMASON"

I have long felt that an official publication of the Grand Lodge would
fill a great need and serve the best interests of Masonry in this jurisdiction.
Heretofore such questions as editing, publishing, format, content,
mailing, and the means of defraying costs erected a collective obstacle
which seemed insurmountable in view of the fact that we had no indica ·
tion of how ~uch a publication would be received by the brethren.
Last year Brother New~omb Candee, Chairman of the Correspondence Committee, came to me with the suggestion that the report of his
committee be issued quarterly instead of annually. After considerable
discussion we worked out a plan whereby this quarterly edition would
also contain newsworthy items of Masonic activity in this jurisdiction
and articles of general Masonic interest by writers of recognized ability,
all at a cost which would not too greatly exceed the appropriation
granted the committee.
Thus was born "California Freemason", the first serious attempt at
an official publication by your Grand Lodge.
Brother Candee and the members of his committee deserve our thanks
for their work in this undertaking. It is a modest beginning, because of
the limitations of money and the time which could be devoted by a volunteer staff.
The fundamental policy of "no advertising" was adopted at the outset. There are several reasons for this. First, experience demonstrates
that individuals and firms who place ads in fraternal publications with
limited circulation too often consider them in the light of donations. It
does not comport with the dignity of our Grand Lodge to be placed in

76

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

that ppsition in the eyes of the profane. Secondly. it would involve an
organization for soliciting ads, bookkeeping, billing,' etc .. which was outside our scope. And, thirdly. it was felt that our publication would find
greater favor with the brethren in its present compact form.
Whatever may be the future of "California Freemason," we are
firmly of the opinion that the policy of "no advertising" is sound and
should be continued.
It is likely that a majority of the brethren have not even seen the
magazine. Our limited funds permitted the printing of only 20.000
copies of each edition. These were mailed to the Lodges in bulk on a
pro rata membership basis for distribution by the Secretary.
On the other hand, we have been gratified with the widespread and
enthusiastic response. To test its reception and to form a base for planning its future, we encl.osed with the Summer edition a return card, on
which we asked if the reader desired to have it continued; if he preferred to pay a subscription charge and have it mailed direct; and we
provided a space for remarks and suggestions.
A survey of the replies is enlightening. Approximately 99% of the
replies requested that the magazine be continued, while 95% wishe? to
subscribe and have it mailed direct. Under remarks and suggestions
the comments were many and varied, mostly having to do with the content of the publication.
Although the number of replies could not be considered a true crosssection of the entire membership, nevertheless I consider it a sufficient
indication of the wishes of those who have seen and read the magazine.
The old adage "Make haste slowly" applies in this matter. Another
year of publication along the lines presently followed will place us on
firmer ground before we consider any substantial expansion. However,
it seems feasible to work out a system for subscripti?ns and direct mail.
ing.
All such details are better left in the hands of those who will have
them in charge.
I therefore, recommend ( 1 ) that the publication known as "Califomfa Freemason" be continued; and ( 2) that an appropriation of
$8,000.00 be made to defray its cost, with the understanding, of course,
that if receipts from subscriptions, plus this appropriation, should exceed
all costs, any unexpended remainder shall revert to the general funds
of Grand Lodge.

North Main Street. This is the second meeting place of Los Angeles
Lodge No. 42, which celebrated its centennial this year, and the first
Masonic Hall in that city.
A committee of the Lodge and I held a meeting with some of the
City Officials and a stay of execution of the order of demolition has
been granted until May 1, 1955.
The building is at present the property of the city. The state has
purchased old historical buildings and sites in the immediate neighborhood and made them a part of the Plaza de Los Angeles Historical
Monument. It has been suggested and there is a possibility that the
state may purchase the property so that it may be preserved and included in the monument. ·
Across the street is the original Plaza Church and nearby is the
Plaza. Leading off the Plaza is famous Olvera Street. These are all a
part of the Historical Monument. It is and will continue to be a mecc2
for thousands of tourists.
I feel that the Masons of California will want this building preserved,
not only for its historical significance, but as a reminder to all visitors
that Masons played an important role in building the great city which,
in its early days, centered around the old Plaza.
I, therefore, recommend that the incoming Grand Master be authorized and directed to appoint a special committee to keep in close touch
with all developments relating to this property, to follow up the possibility of its purchase by the state as a part of the monument, and to
present recommendations for its preservation, in some form, as a Masonic Memorial.

DECISIONS

Many questions involving the interpretation and application of our
Regulations have been submitted to me during the year. In some I felt
the law was so clear that reference to the proper section was sufficient
to answer the inquiry.
The remainder seemed to call for some new interpretation or initial

GRAND MAsTER's DECISION No. 1

GRAND MAsTER's DECISION No. 3

May a Lodge furnish to a bona fide printer and mailing service a
roster of its members for the purpose of having mailed to the members
the Lodge Bulletin or Trestle Board?
The answer is "yes."
In such a case there is a duty which devolves upon the Master of
the Lodge to make sure that the roster is used solely for Masonic purposes. ( R.D. 732.)
GRAND MASTER's DECISION No. 4

May a Mason, in the conduct of his business, comprising a restaurant
and a bar, ever himself act as a bartender?
The answer is "no." (Drapeau Edict, Rulings 14 and 35, pages 30,
37, 326, Grand Lodge Proceedin gs 1952.)
One who becomes a barkeeper shall be deemed guilty of un-Mason ic
conduct (R.D. 210, 887).

Is it proper for a Lodge to publish, or cause to be published in a
publication distributed among the profane, official communications from
the Grand Master or official communications from the Grand Lodge to
the Lodge?
In some cases it would be permissible, such as for our Public Schools

would not be permissible, as for example in the case of work of the
Grievance Committe e or applications for Degrees.
It is understoo d that the Grand Master will designate as confidential
those matters which should not be circulated among the profane.

GRAND MASTER's DEc1sION No. 8

GRAND MAsTER's DEasION No. 9

Is a professional gambler eligible to receive the Degrees of Masonry?
The answer is "no."
Gambling is a Masonic offense ( R.D. 739). The proposed applicant, being a profession al gambler and employed as such in a gambling
establishment, does not come under the tongue of good report ( R.D.
739. 740, 875.)

GRAND MASTER's DECISION No. 11

What corrective action should be taken in respect of an applicant
for the Degrees who, within one year of his rejection by one Lodge,
applied to another Lodge. stating. inadvertently in his application that
more than one year had elapsed from his rejection, and which other
Lodge thereupon proceeded to eiect, initiate and pass the applicant before the illegality was discovered?
The second Lodge most correctly denied advancement since the applicant had not legally been elected, initiated or passed. ( 219, 704 R.D.)
But, since it is impossible from a practical standpoint to take away
what the applicant had received, the following procedure should be followed in this case: the second Lodge should tender to the Lodge which
had rejected the applicant the fees for the first and second Degrees, and
should return to the applicant the fees for the Third Degree. If the
applicant desires advancement, he should apply for the Third Degree
with the usual reference and ballot (219, 704, 708 R.D.).

activity, with charity i!:nplications, contrary to Section 795a, R.D.

of June 3, 1954. fo this it was pointed out that the proposed plan would

GRAND MASTER'S DECISION No. 13

May a Lodge lease and hold meetings in premises wherein the
• American Legion at their meetings sell and dispense liquor to members
df their organization under a permit from the State Board of Equalization for that purpose?
The answer is "no." ( R.D. 596.)
While this may ·he said to be on the fringes of legality, so far as
Masonic law is concerned, and while almost all the liquor would be
removed from the premises after the meetings of the American Legion,
still the Edict of Grand Master Warren, 1936 page 21, and the Edict
of Grand Master Gist, 1934 pages 26-27, indicate the advisability of
not leasing the premises unless the business of selling liquor could be
eliminated from the premises.
GRAND MASTER'S DECISION No. 14

Does the prohibition of Question 13 in the Application for Degrees,
as amended 1953, apply to the so-called "Square Clubs," the prerequisite of membershi·p wherein is that a person be a Master Mason?
The answer is "yes."
This ruling of the Grand Master should not be construed as approval of any so-called Masonic Clubs.
Considerafion has been given to the ruling of Past Grand Master
Claude Morrison (R.D. 494b). He was not ruling, however, in respect
of the action of Grand Lodge in 1953, at which time it would appear
the intent of Grand Lodge was to extend the prohibition to "any Lodge.
order, oc organization" the prerequisite of membership wherein is that
a person be a Master Mason. While it is true the requirement is further
conditioned, to a somewhat formulistic extent, on a "Degree" or "initiation," still the basic intent seems to include a social club. This follows
from the plain reading of the Question 13 as adopted by Grand Lodge
in 1953, and wherein there are no exceptions noted. It would seem that
if a social club were to be excepted, then the language would have
clearly so set forth.
