GRAND MASTER'S DECISION No. 16
Should a Lodge return fees to a Candidate who commenced but did
not complete initiation and was denied advancem ent on objection by
reason of physical unfitness?
The answer is "yes."
The Lodge should return the fees to the Candidate on expiration of
sixty days from the meeting at which the Master reported the fact of
objection. (Drapeau Edict 28, Grand Lodge Proceedin gs 1952, pages
34, 326.)
The Candidate did not attain the status of an initiate because he
did not receive the lecture. The situation presented , therefore, is similar
to objection made before initiation. Conseque ntly, the fee should be
returned as provided in R.D. 237. (Drapeau Edict 28, Proceedin gs 1952,
pages 35, 330.)
GRAND MAsTER's DECISION No. 17
Are Trustees of a Lodge "officers" within the meaning of such as
a Master may appoint in the event of a vacancy prior to expiration of
a term?
The answer is "no."
The Trustees of a Lodge are required as such to "always be under
its control." and to act "as the Lodge shall direct." ( R.D. 154, 600, 601.)
They are intended to be "provided for in a standing resolution."
The resolution of the Lodge involved assumes that the Trustees will
be elected by the Lodge. It is silent as to vacancies. In this connection.
reference is made to an approved form of standing resolution, supplied
by the Grand Secretary on request, which provides the procedure whereby vacancies shall be filled, and this by election.
It is suggested that the Lodge in question adopt and follow this
approved form of standing resolution.

Is the tiler's room and preparatio n room a part of the Lodge room?

The answer to this question is "no." ( R.D. 422.) No member may

or some other imperative reason should be pleaded.
The "Lodge room," contemplated in R.D. 422, is the "box" outside ·
of which are located the tiler's room and the preparatio n room. Obviously, this must be so since it is the duty of the tiler to guard the Lodge

GRAND MAsTER's DEasION No. 19
May an organizati on, the prerequisite of membership wherein is that
they :be Masons, sponsor the sale of tickets for a public circus to be held
on January 177
The answer is "no."
Since January 17 is a Sunday, the sale of tickets for the circus ~ould
violate Section 790-792, Ross Digest.
It is apparent from the information submitted that in the eyes of the
public there would be a sale of tickets for a Sunday public circus by an
organization Masonic in character. The Masonic members of that organization may not thus bring discredit upon Masonry.
Note also the general prohibition against raising fonds for Masonic
charities by public entertainm ent. R.D. 795-795 (a).
GRAND MASTER'S DECISION No. 20
Is conviction of a felony, prior to application for Degrees, ground
for automatic expulsion?
The answer is "no." (Trial Record No. 1191, 1950: Trial Record
No. 1327, 1952.)
We are not concerned with the question whether the facts involved
in the conviction of a felony, suffered prior to application for Degrees,
constitute grounds for Masonic trial. A Mason can be tried for moral
offenses committed ;b efore initiation. ( R.D. 753.)
Apparentl y the Master of Florence Lodge has misunderstood what
some member of the Grievance Committe e may have stated was the law.
From the above, it is clear that a prior conviction does not, in and of
itself, give rise to automatic expulsion. But the basis for the prior conviction may be grounds for trials if such basis involved a moral offense.
(Your inquiry was written while you were still Master of the Lodge,
hence the reference to the Master of Florence Lodge.)
GRAND MASTER'S DECISION No. 21
Must a Charity Committee of a Lodge, composed of the Master and

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

the Wardens, report through the Master at each Stated Meeting all
payments of charity since the last Stated Meeting?
The answer is "yes" ( R.D. 891 ) .
It is required, moreover, that the Master file with the Secretary for
use at each Stated Meeting the names of the recipients and the amounts
paid since the last Stated Meeting. ( R.D. 782: 202.)
In making the oral report at the Stated Meeting, the Master, speaking for the Charity Committee, may report merely the sum total expended, and refer any interested and proper person to the detailed report
mentioned, on file with the Secretary, for further information.
In addition to the above decisions it has been necessary for me to
take action in certain cases. I suspended the Master of a Lodge from
office for his failure to report or give any detailed accounting to the
Lodge of the amounts and recipients of Lodge funds in excess of $4.000,
which he disbursed for relief. He was repeatedly warned during the
year by the Inspector that such a report and accounting was required.
It was reported to me that on one such occasion the Master demanded
that the Inspector show him wherein the law made such a requirement.
It was further reported to me that, on being questioned, the Master
stated that he paid out some of the funds in cash, while others were
handled through his personal bank account, but that he had destroyed
check stubs and canceled checks. He offered as an excuse for his actions
that it was all supposed to be confidential: that this was customary procedure in his Lodge: and that some of the Past Masters had advised
him that his procedure was proper.
When the situation was brought to my attention late last year, I
wrote the Master directing him to comply with the instructions of the
Inspector. This he failed to do and I suspended him from office and
ordered the Inspector to begin a thorough investigation, which was to
include a further effort to have the Master show evidence that the funds
were properly disbursed.
When the date for the annual installation of officers neared and no
conclusive report had reached me, I ordered the installation postponed
to give the Master further time to submit an accounting. This postponement was ordered, of course, to avoid the installation of his successor
while he was under suspension, thus depriving him of the rank and title
of Past Master. However, I was besieged with requests by the Master
and Wardens-elect to allow the installation to be held on the scheduled
date and was informed by the suspended Master that it was also his
wish. With the assurance that the suspended Master clearly understood
the penalty he would suffer, I rescinded the order of postponement and
the installation was held.
The subsequent report of the investigation failed to show any mate-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

85

rial evidence, other than the statement of the Master, as to how the
funds had .been disbursed.
I have not ordered that charges be preferred against this Master.
feeling that deprivation of the rank and title of Past Master was sufficient punishment for his derelictions.
I addressed a letter to the newly installed Master, outlining the
proper procedure in the use of Lodge funds for relief and ordered that
it be read to the Lodge and spread upon the minutes.
In another Lodge, objection was made to me against the installation
of the Master-elect. Because of previous reports which had reached me
of lack of harmony in this Lodge, I ordered postponement of the installation. I directed Guy B. Mize, Assistant Grand Lecturer, to make a thorough investigation, and upon receiving his enlightening report I ordered
the Master of the Lodge to summons the members to a special meeting,
at which Brother Mize was present as my representattive and read to
the Lodge a letter from me. I am happy to report that as a result the
installation was subsequently held without any objection and harmony
appears to have been restored. I record my appreciation of the able and
conclusive services of Brother Mize.
During the recent political campaign ·a candidate for public office,
who was a member of one of our Lodges, broadcast over the state a
letter seeking support. In a portion of the letter these words were used:
"To my Brothers of the Masonic Fraternity I say." Following that, the
letter went on at length to appeal for the votes of Masons because of
his membership.
This was •such a blatant disregard for the rules of propriety and
the laws of the Institution that I ordered Masonic charges preferred
against him.
Other instances were brought to my attention where a candidate's
membership in the fraternity was used, one way or another, in appeals
for votes, but in none of these by the candidate himself. The propriety
of the methods used · in some of these instances was questionable, although I did not feel warranted in directing that any charges be preferred.
I feel it my duty to call the attention of the brethren to this growing
tendency to misuse membership in the_fraternity in political campaigns.
It has been argued that, when a candidate for ptJ1blic office is a Mason,
his candidacy and membership in the fraternity should be brought to
the attention of his brethren, because his election would serve the best
interests of the community and state, and we should not be too technical
ff our Regulations are violated in the process.
The only .possible justification for such reasoning is that the end in ·
itself may be good: but it is pure sophistry to argue that, to attain that
end, we are justified in using means which do violence to the proprieties
and the laws.

CONCLUSION

I wish that I were gifted with the foresight and wisdom to look
ahead on the road we shall follow in the years immediately before us
and tell you now how we can plan to avoid those pitfalls and by-paths
which would make our progress a difficult one.
However, I can say to you with the utmost confidence that with
these lamps to guide our feet and these landmarks to point the way we
shall not stray too far or fall too hard:
To believe that to make innovations in the body of Masonry is to
turn our backs on the wisdom of the past and pursue a dangerous course.
To believe in and submit to the patiently and carefully taken decision of the majority.
To believe that we are our brother's keeper-not only because moral
law and fraternal precept say so, but because it is the dictate of our
conscience.
To believe that there is a higher law which governs our lives and
that the way to understand it is to ask for and receive the guidance of
Almighty God.
·
Thus, my brethren, I believe that our great fraternity will move
calmly and SlJCCessfully on into an unending future.

REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
OF THE MASONIC HOMES

As we reported · to you last year, the care of the aged senile is a
matter of great concern to us and we are continuing to give careful
study to the matter of proper custodial care for those persons who are
not dangerous to themselves or others.
The Trustees have in previous years reported the increased number
of applications made for admission to the Home at Decoto and the present year is no exception. A study of the residents' figures and admissions
will indicate that there has been a steady increase.
It is also noticeable that applications are being made at a more advanced age and in all probability both factors are due to the economic
situation and the change in the State law regarding the care of the
senile aged.
Plans are being made to temporarily at least meet the increased
requirement by converting one of the floors at Decoto to give an added
27 beds. If the trend does not change we shall be forced to give serious
consideration to the erection of a new building at Decoto if we are to
meet our responsibility to our aged Brethren, their wives and widows.

GENERAL

The Board urges all members of the Fraternity to read carefully the
reports of Superintendent James R. Eubanks of the Home for the Aged
at Decato, and Superintendent Robert M. Henry of the Home for Children at Covina which are a part of this report.

FINANCE

During the past year, the Homes have been able to operate within
the estimates made. Each year has seen a rise in operating costs due to
general conditions~ The expanded medical program, the inclusion of our
employees under Social Security and other factors ha_ve materially added
to costs.
During the coming year, we will have additional expenses because
of the inaugu~ation of our retirement program for employees at both
Homes. This program approved by Grand Lodge in 1947 is necessary
to keep both plants staffed with adequate and comjJetent personnel.
The generosity of the Brethren in their response to the Endowment
Fund and the splendid work done by the Investment Committee has
greatly increased the income from securities. This has made it possible
to reduce the per capita levy from $1.00 to 75c for 1952-53 and 1953-54
and to 50c for 1954-55.
It must be remembered, however, that the per capita levied this year
will not be payable until August, 1955 and will provide funds to meet
operations for the fiscal year 1955-56. It is very difficult to estimate our
income and expenses two years hence when we must rely on such a
variable as the number of applicants entering Masonry and who provide
us with over 40% of our income. Consequently, we must consider our
projected budget for the coming year as a guide. Our best estimate indicates that with only a 50c per capita this year, we may face a deficit
of $50,000.00 unless the number of candidates exceeds that of the year
just closed.
We, therefore, recommend the continuance of the per capita levy of
50c to ·be paid with the returns of August, 1955.

In summary it can be said, therefore, that the operation in the past
year and particularly throughout the first nine months of 1954 has shown
an increasing satisfaction to doctors and patients and is steadily decreasing costs to the Home itself due to the more efficient operation of the
service and the avoidance of expensive hospitalization.

Early in the year the Board was confronted with the problem of
either maintaining the North. East and South elevators at a high cost.
or replacing them with new, modern equipment: the latter course was
decided upon.
Some difficulty was encountered with the Building Department of
the County of Alameda with reference to a proposed extension of rise
to serve a new fifth floor level. It appears now that the problems will
be resolved and this work will be allowed to proceed soon.
Work is under way on the East and South elevators: all the new
equipment should be in operation in the near future.

MEDICAL SERVICE AT DECOTO

The operation during the past year has had the benefit of the previous year's experience and is proceeding more smoothly.
During the year 1953 a total of 1739 patients were seen at the
Decoto Home Clinic, averaging between 126 and 163 patients per month.
In the Decoto Home Hospital. 2098 patients were seen, with a
spread of between 119 and 300 patients per month.
An average of about 50 patients per month were sent to the Palo
Alto Clinic for a total year's average of 658, and during the year 1953,
57 patients were admitted to the Palo Alto Hospital. Up to date in 1954,
the number of patients hospitalized has been -definitely less than the
previous year because of the improved liaison between the operation of
the Decoto Home Hospital and the doctors of the Palo Alto Clinic.
·A great many more co~ditions are taken care of in the Home's Infirmary and Hospital rather than patients being hospitalized in Palo
Alto. At the beginning of this service there was a considerable backlog
of surgical diseases requiring operations. This backlog has now been
largely caught up with and now is mostly what could :be called a "maintenance problem." This can be expected to level off during the present
year to a point where it may be anticipated to continue in the future.
The residents themselves are learning how to properly use the
medical facilities that are offered to them and the doctors are becoming
more and more familiar with the peculiar problems which are encountered in a home largely devoted to people of this age.
It must be said in any consideration of this operation, that it could
not be successful without the efficient work of the nursing director, Miss
Elizabeth Payne, who has extraordinary aptitudes for dealing with
older patients and her cordial and cooperative relationship with the
doctors has been a major factor in the rather outstanding success of this
operation as shown.

Referred to Committee on Finance.

Report of Superinten dent-Deco to Home
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
Brethren: I hereby present for your consideratio n this, my 13th
Annual Report as Superintend ent of the Masonic Home at Decoto for
the year ending July 31, 1954.
The population of the Home on August 1, 1953 was 111 men and
181 women, a total of 292. Thirty-nine women, average age 77 years
and twenty-nine men average age of 75 years were admitted, during
the year. During the same period 22 women, average age 82.68 and
17 men average age 82.35 passed away, 3 men and·2 women were withdrawn, population on August 1st 1954 is 121 men, 196 women, a total
of 317. Included in this number are 11 married couples.

Age groups such as are represented above, will of necessity require

Recently a new department has been added to our hospital facilities.
Modern dental equipment has been installed which enables us to render
a more complete and satisfactory service to all the members of the Home.
Dr. William O'Connor, of Hayward, who has been our dentist for 20
years or more, will be in charge of this department.
Through the thoughtfuln ess and generosity of Mrs. Marble, of
Loomis, Calif.. mother of Marvin C. Peterson. a member of Eureka
Lodge No. 16, we have in use in our ·h ospital a Hoyer Lifter.
This fine contribution makes it possible for our nurses and attendants
to handle our infirm and paraletic patients more efficiently.
We had hoped to have t'he new elevators which were delivered to the
Home some time ago, installed long before now. The installation has
been delayed due to the fact that we have been unable to secure a building permit from the Alameda County Building Inspector's office. We

believe, however, that the building permit matter will be straightened
out in the near future, and that work on the elevators will then go forward.
It is interesting to note that 1879 Masonic brethren, their wives,
widows and mothers have availed themselves of the facilities of the
Home since it opened in 1899.
3947 signed our guest register during the year. Represented in this

Caracoz, Venezuela; Lima, Peru; Canada, Germany, France, Stockholm, Sweden: and Egypt. were also represented .
Mrs. Esther Essieva, who has been serving as Matron of the Home
for the past two years, resigned on June 30 to assume the important
duties of housewife. Mrs. Maude Teass of San Francisco, was appointed Matron and assumed the responsibilities of that very important assignment on July 1, 1954. During Mrs. Teass short tenure, ~he has
proven herself not only qualified and capable, but also cooperative and
congenial, and through her fair consideration of all the members' requests
and her sympathetic understandi ng of their problems, she is rapidly
gaining the admiration, confidence and respect of all the members of
the Home.
Brother Paul Shipman, who so ably filled the office of Assistant
Superintend ent of our Home for two years, was appointed Superintendent of the Masonic and Eastern Star Home of Oregon and took
over the duties of that assignment June 1, 1954.
The vacancy caused by Brother Shipman's resignation was filled
by t'he appoint;nen t of Brother Gail David, a membe~ of Piedmont
Lodge No. 521. Although the duties of this office are vaned and numerous, Brother David has made very satisfactory progress. We believe
in a very short time he will have everything under control.
Under the able leadership of Brother Hildebrand, Paul Reichert,
William Emmal and Reverend Cecil Rhoades, our accounting, commissary, culinary and devotional departments are operating very satisfactorily. There is a report about the Home that Reverend Rhoades is
leaving us on September 15. He has been appointed Pastor of a church
in Pennsylvani a.

The many .fine programs which were brought to the Home during
the past year by the lodges, Eastern Star Chapters and friends, are too
numerous to record here. We would like, however, to make special
mention of three programs which were, in our opinion, very outstanding .
August 15, 1953, the East Bay Matron's Association, Mrs. Clarabell
Migs, ·Past Matron, chairman; held their annual reception in honor of
Worthy Grand Matron Gilma Vick Moyer. Following the reception
a very interesting and enjoyable program was presented. At the conclusion of the ceremonies, Mrs. Essie Hickman, Past Matron of the San
Ramon Valley Chapter, announced that the good ladies of the associa-·
tion had presented the Home with 10, 152 jars of jams and jellies and
3,814 jars of assorted relishes, fruit juices, fruit cocktail, etc.
August 15th, Grand Master Arthur M. Warren, in company with
his gracious wife, made his official visit to the Home. The afternoon was
spent inspecting the various departments of the Home. In the evening
a reception was held in the auditorium in honor of Grand Master and
Mrs. Warren. Th·ey were escorted to the stage and introduced to the
members of the Home. His address which followed, was interesting
and certainly appreciated very much by the Home. Following Grand
Master Warren's address, he and his party were escorted to seats
reserved for them. Mrs. Loretta Hyman then took over and presented
a delightful program she had so painstaking ly developed for the occasion. Refreshments were served during the fellowship that followed.
This gave the Grand Master an excellent opportunity to meet and greet
the members of the Home.
The East Bay Masters and Wardens Association, headed by their
President, Wake.field Taylor, made their annual visit to the Home on
August 2, enjoyed a barbecue which they had prepared for them. They
then presented an excellent program which the residents of the Home
enjoyed very much.
Devotional services are held each Sunday at the Home. I am sure
you will agree that a word of commendation here to those Reverend
gentlemen who journey out to the Home each Sunday and bring such

.

comforting messages to the residents of the Home, is not entirely out
of place.
The Thursday evening programs which are provided by RKO,
Columbia Pictures, United Artists, Warner Brothers and Twentieth
Century Fox Film Distributing Companies of San Francisco, are greatly
llJ>preciated and enjoyed by the residents of the Home. To these .fine
organization s go our sincere thanks and appreciation.
The Trustees, Grand Master, Grand Secretary and other Grand
Lodge Officers, have made periodical visits to the Home during the
year. We appreciate these visits and urge their continuance, knowing
that the Home is going to benefit as a result of their visits.
In conclusion, the Home staff and myself wish to extend to our loyal
employees our sincere thanks for their loyal services. We also want
to assure the loyal members of the Home that we appreciate the fine
servi~e they are rendering to the Home.

Report of the Superintendent-Covina Home
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
It is a privilege and a pleasure to present to you my sixth annual
report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home for Children at Covina,
for the year ending July 31, 1954.

sports program of their respective schools. This year the Home enjoyed
~ving the Student Body President of Charter Oak Grammar School:
Vice-President of the Student Body, and Girls' League President of
Covina High School; and the Student Body President at Mount San
Antonio College. Through these mediums our boys and girls and children of the community join in social events at the Home, such as dances,
picnics, barbecues, and swim parties. These social activities are planned
by the children; the older groups taking the responsibility of their own
special affairs, with the help and guidance of the houseparent. Attendance at Sunday School and church is the major part of our religious
training program; every child is encouraged to participate in the activities of the church of his choice. Various sports activities such as hikes,
weekend camping and fishing expeditions are frequently planned and
are supervised under our recreations program. Instruction in singing,
piano, ,a nd ballet, is optional with the individual child, and is a part of
our cultural training and development program. At the May meeting
of the Los Angeles Board of Relief. children of the ballet class presented
a program of their dances, and at the Big Family Christmas Party entertained our guests with a delightful and colorful dance program. At
frequent intervals throughout the year, films of special educational value
are presented to the children. Awards are given to those attaining high
scholastic grades in their school work; in this direction it is fitting that
we offer our sincere appreciation to The Westerners' Masonic Club of
Twentieth Century-Fox, for their kindness in including our boys and
girls in The Westerners' Scholastic Contest held each year. From kindergarten to the twelfth grade, seven Covina Home children won awards
in the 1953 contest, and attended the Award Dinner at the Twentieth
Century-Fox Studios. Two of our senior boys received special honors:
Harold Eller, '55, was sponsored by Sunshine Post No. 251, American
legion, to attend Boys' State at Sacramento, and Charles Burkhalter,
because of his outstanding work in the Masonic Pioneers 4-H Club,
was chosen to attend the Conference of 4-H Junior Leaders at the University of California, Davis Campus.

IMPROVEMENT PROGRAM

We have ·placed the water softener equipment in the boiler room and
installed an additional sprinkling system to increase the value and use
of our pasture land. Each room in the children's dormitories is being
repainted. To the main kitchen however, we turned most of our improvement endeavors, resulting in one of the most up-to-date kitchens in the
institution field. As replacement equipment we installed an electric
dumb waiter and a modern dish scraper-dish washer combination, with
stainless steel stacking counter; a Hobart thirty-pound capacity vegetable peeler, equipped with brushes for washing vegetables; two Hobart
electric mixers--one ten quart size and one thirty-quart size; and a
Toledo electric meat slicing machine. Three stationary and three roll
tables were covered with stainless steel and a stainless steel apron was
added to the serving counter. A complete set of professional cutlery
was purchased and all walk-in refrigerators and pantries were given a
fresh coat of paint.

REPOR T OF
MASON IC HOME S ENDOW MENT BOARD
1954

To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Masonic Homes Endowm ent Board takes great pleasure in
presenting, herewith, its twenty-s econd annual report covering the period from August 1. 1953, to July 31, 1954, inclusive.
The heart should thrill with joy and pride from the activities demonstrated by the Craft, over the years, in behalf of this great overall
Charity. No finer example of progress and accumulative activities
could be shown in any phase of our work than in the Endowm ent
Board program .
While the Endowm ent Fund was created by Grand Lodge in 1910,
the Endowm ent Board was not born until 1933; then, by Constitu tional
Amendment, such a Board was created and was charged with the responsibility of disseminating information about our two great Homes;
for the children at Covina, and our older folk at Decato.
Building an adequate endowm ent for anything is no small task.
When we consider the few short years of our activity and the limited
number of people, compara tively, which ·by the very nature of our institution are a part of this program , we may well be proud of the wonderful progress. After all, it was just an IDEA, but one which was founded
basically and fundame ntally and which has grown by leaps and bounds
into a practical REALIT Y, from a few dollars to approxim ately $5.600,000.00. Fortunat ely, it has that perpetui ty which is necessar y for the
success of any such program . We are graduall y, yet surely, getting
toward that goal so that in the future, we may realize a sufficient income
to support our two splendid Homes.
THE DEVEL OPMEN T AND PROGR ESS
It might be well for us to take stock and see how it has been possible to accomplish the results in such a few short years. First, let us
give credit to those who not only originate d the idea, but also to those
who took it seriously, served on the Board, and were willing to give
further time and thought to its development.
Things don't usually happen, people make them happen, and so it
is with the Endowm ent Fund. The Board members took their work seriously, devotedly, and enthusiastically, and have been able to show
progress. The Jurisdiction is divided into thirteen general areas. To
each area is assigned the responsibility of the educatio nal program in
that particula r district. Pamphle ts telling the story of our Homes have

been distributed and are available to all Lodges. These have reached
the in~ividual member of the Craft. His interest and his opportunity
for participation have been created. The Masters, Officers of the Lodges,
and the Endowment Fund Chairmen have made it possible that further
information be obtained and intimate stories of the activities have been
available. Meetings of the Districts have aided materially. We are very

Last but not least. the very effective work of the Most Worshipful

all of these have added to the success of our year's work.

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
For the past several years it has been the aim of the Board of Control
to bring to the craft the full realization of the importance of the work
performed by our Boards of Relief and our Employment Bureaus. For
some reason we have failed to reach a large majority of those who should
be interested. The message has been given at our Masonic Breakfasts
throughout the state. Every year during the communication of Grand
Lodge we have given the message to you by means of this report in the
hope that you would carry it back to your lodges. The ordinances of
Grand Lodge require that certain facts and figures be presented at each
communication.
During the past Masonic Year our Boards of Relief and Employ~
ment Bureaus have rendered services to hundreds upon hundreds of our
brethren, their widows and orphans. The value of this service within
our jurisdiction must be emphasized to the members of the craft.
Our Boards of Relief were established to aid the distressed among
our sojourning brethren and it is our duty to see to it that our needy
brethren are not permitted to suffer or to be made a burden upon others.
In this report you will find that during the past Masonic year nearly
$60,000 has been advanced for .actual relief, that our Boards of Relief
have been responsible for and have conducted nearly a thousand
Masonic funerals, that they have called upon more than 26,000 sick and
distressed sojourning Masons, their widows and orphans. This gives
but a brief pjcture of the volume of work of the 18 secretaries of our
Boards of Relief. To these men goes little credit from the craft. Of
necessity their work must be quietly performed. Names of recipients
cannot be used although on many occasions the Board of Control has
cited case histories believing that they would be of interest to the craft.
Secretaries must be continually on the watch for imposters. They must
be careful in the management of the affairs of their office so that no one
who is entitled to relief be turned away with his needs unmet. The very
nature of these cases requires the utmost care to insure proper sympathy
and understanding and to prevent embarassment. The Board of Con:.
trol has always operated on the theory that it would rather have· secre~
taries err on the side of generosity than to permit one Mason, his widow
or orphan to go away without receiving the help to which he ii;; entitled.
The Board of Control is pleased to report that in the administration
and supervision of our 18 Boards of Relief the year was without incident.
The utmost cooperation prevailed between the secretaries of our Boards
of R,elief, the managers of our Employment Bureaus and the Board of
Control. We praise the work that has been accomplished during the
past Masonic year as we have done on many occasions in the past.
Many of the men in this work are now growing old in the service of

112

113

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Masonry. Serious consideration must be given in the not too distant
future to the problem of securing others who will be equal in calibre to
the type of men who have represented us over the past years. Ill health
and advancing age is a fact that we must all face, and this is a problem
which some of our Boards of Relief now have directly in front of them.
It will be difficult to find replacements for the experience that they have
gained through years of contact, through the personal interest which
they have developed and for their honest and sincere love of the work
in which they are engaged. I am sure that it will be of interest to you
that over the years during which our Boards of Relief have been in oper..
ation there have been very few changes in the personnel of the secre..
taries of these boards. For some reason once a Mason becomes inter..
ested in the work of relief he seems to find no other avenue which gives
him as much personal satisfaction as to continue day after day, year
after year in following and relieving the distress of his brother Masons.

Were we to charge the fee allowed commercial employment agencies
within the state, our Employment Bureaus would have earned $249,453.

REPORT OF OuR BOARDS OF RELIEF

Since the close of the past Masonic year all 18 Boards have placed
on file with the Board of Control a complete record of the activities of
their office. This is required by the ordinances. All of the reports which
have been submitted have been audited by qualified accountants and
have been carefully analyzed by fhe Board of Control. During the past
year the report of our Boards of Relief shows as follows:
Advanced for relief --------------------$59,385.00
Funerals conducted ·-------············
951
Total calls made ·····-···-··-·-···········
26,497
Sick calls ·······-···-···-··-·············-----9,636
Investigations conducted ··----···-··
476
Relief calls ···-·-----····-·-·-···-··------·-···
6,305
Miscellaneous calls -·-·······-···-------·
10,080
Many of our Boards of Relief maintain Blood Banks for the benefit
of our Masonic Brethren and their families. During the past year these
boards made the following report:
Units of Blood Donated........................ 2,617
Units of Blood Withdrawn ..................2,745
This has resulted in a direct saving to our brethren of $71.785.00.
REPORT OF OuR EMPLOYMENT BUREAUS

We maintain seven Employment Bureaus within the State, extending
from San Diego on the south to the East Bay on fhe north. All of these
bureaus have filed their audited reports with the Board of Control as is
required. From these reports the following statistics have been compiled:
Registered for employment during the past Masonic year.... 8,275
Placed in employment _________...................................................2,672
Positions offered by employers................................................ 5,586

You will not from these figures that during the past year the employ..
ment services have passed through a rather difficult period. We feel
that some explanation might serve as a guide so that you may better
understand t'he problems which these bureaus are now facing.
After the signing of the Truce there was considerable slump in em..
ployment. Contracts were cancelled and men were laid off by fhe thou ..
sands. Placements dropped consistently every month until December
of 1953, and naturally applications for employment increased. Begin..
ning with January 1954 employment began to increase, slowly of course
but encouraging. Many of our male applicants were in the higher age
group and these during times of general unemployment are hard to place.
Unfortunately, when conditions improved and we were getting more calls
for men, we found a shortage of truly skilled job candidates in practi..
cally all fields. During wartime employers got along as best fhey could
with what help was available. There had been no training programs of
any magnitude to make up for the shortage in many desirable skills.
This condition is general and even the trade unions have the same diffi ..
culty. Young men, either out of service or out of college, are not satisfied
to take training in any particular field but are anxious to get started to
work. Corporations now seem to be interested in young people whom
they can train for the future. Men and women with a college back..
ground can still find work, if they are satisfied with the wages offered,
and too often they are not. Many employment inducements are offered,
permanent emtJloyment, health plans, retirement, etc., and in many cases
the selection is made directly from the college graduating class. Con ..
sequently, many openings never reach the open market to be filled.
Closed shop contracts of many labor unions are another bar to our secur..
ing employment for our people.
We are convinced after many years of experience in this work that
the fraternal angle of our service has been responsible for many of our
placements. Many competeot people do register with us for employment
and many employers prefer to deal with us when they need help. A
satisfied employer can be our best booster if we are able to give him the
kind of help that he is looking for. We prefer not to fill vacancies with
incompetent people merely for the sake of making a placement as this
may tend to antagonize an employer. We know of many instances where
our people, being advanced in age, have been placed through our employ..
ment bureaus and we are confident that they never would have found
employment otherwise.
We have a heavy listing of men who, through compulsory retire..
ment at 65, are not able to make ends meet on the small pension they
receive. These men are hard to place today on account of the economic

situation, whereas, a few years ago we were able to place a great many
of them, and employers were glad to get them for their reliability.
One of our bureaus reports that it receives very few calls for female
help except in the clerical field, and it reports that the majority of its
placements during the past year was stenographers mostly in the higher
salary bracket. This year it has had more high school graduates register
for this type of work than in the combined total of the past ten years.
This is 'partly due to the fact that in prior years these girls went right
to work for the government after graduation whereas today there are
no positions available due to the rigid curtailment.
This presents the general picture, as we see it, of the conditions
existing within employment bureaus as of today. We do not feel that
there is any immediate hope of any change. It is impossible to create
jobs when there are none available. It is also of interest to note that
while the work of our employment bureaus has dropped off materially
the duties of our Boards of Relief have increased considerably.
When the Board of Control met in Los Angeles in February and
again at its meeting in June in San Francisco, we discussed the problem
with our employment managers and informed them that the Board of
Control was watching the current situation very carefully and was
weighing the advisability of discontinuing our Masonic Employment
Bureaus.
This statement does not mean that we have reached any final conclusion on the matter but is simply mentioned to call attention to the fact
that the Board of Control recognizes the problems confronting us and
is conscious of the expense in maintaining our Employment Bureaus.

Case No. 1 was from the Masonic Board of Relief of San Francisco
and was for $175.00 advanced to relieve the distress of a brother from
the Grand Lodge of Scotland. Since that time the Grand Secretary of
the Grand Lodge of Scotland has written wherein they state that this
amount is being forwarded to the San Francisco Board. This case is
therefore closed and no recommendation is necessary.
Case No. 2 is a request from the Masonic Board of Relief of the
East Bay for reimbursement in the sum of $150.00.
The sum above mentioned was to pay for the cost of a Masonic
burial of a brother belonging to Innocents Lodge No. 224 of the Grand
Jurisdiction of Scotland. A letter to his lodge brought a reply and
advised that the deceased brother was not in good standing with his
lodge at the time of his death and that the lodge had unanimously agreed
not to reimburse the sum requested.
The Board of Control feels that the secretary used his best judgment
based on the evidence available. It is the opinion of the Board of Control
that even though an error may have been made in providing a Masonic
burial for one who was not in good standing, nevertheless evidence
available at the time seemed to indicate otherwise and that therefore the
Masonic Board of Relief of the East Bay should not be penalized for its
actions.
The Board of Control therefore has recommended to the Finance
Committee that the Masonic Board of Relief of the East Bay be reimbursed in the amount of $150.00.
Case No. 3 is a request for reimbursement from the Masonic Board
of Relief of Santa Monica Bay. A member of Alamo Lodge No. 44 A.
F. & A. M. of the Grand Jurisdiction of Texas received assistance in the
amount of $52.00. Repeated attempts to secure this amount from the
brother's Lodge were without success. The Board of Control therefore
has recommended to the Finance Committee that the Masonic Board of
Relief of Santa Monica Bay be reimbursed in the amount of $52.00.

INTRODUCTION

The .fac~ .that for thirty-five years an ever increasing number of
schools, md1v1duals and organizations have participated in the Masonicsponsored observance of Public Schools Week is in itself a testimonial
of the soundness of this program. The cumulating years only add to the
statur~ an~ e~du~ng qualities of this event which has become recognized
as an institution m the calendars of the public schools of California and
Hawaii .
.For the first time, just prior to the 35th. anniversary of this occasion,
national recognition was given to Public Schools Week when Freedoms
Foundation at historic Valley Forge conferred, on Washington's Birthday. the gold medal "For Outstanding Achievement in Bringing About
a Better Understanding of the American Way of Life." The presentation was made by Dr. Milton Eisenhower. The ceremony was nationally
broadcast.
It is a source of added satisfaction to those who work with Public
Schools Week to see it being adopted by Masonic Grand Lodges in
othe~ states. At the present time similar programs are now being carried
out m many Grand Jurisdictions. A kit of our Public Schools Week
material has been sent to each Grand Lodge in the United States so that
they may have a better knowledge of our program.
Each year, too, the volume of inquiries from outside the jurisdiction
increases and Public Schools Week has become a year round obligation
for the General Committee in keeping up with this correspondence.

SCOPE AND OBJECT.OF PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK
Each year an ever increasing number of our Brethren who serve on
their local Public Schools Week programs know that this event does
. not "just happen." It is the result of long weeks of planning and preparation.
The planning, naturally; starts with the General Committee. It is
the function of this committee to coordinate the programs of the various
local committees, to give them a certain degree of uniformity in order
to gain added force and effect in the over-all campaign.
The General Committee supplies a series of mailings to local committees, a speaker's manual, publicity and radio-TV press books, together with an informative guide to the planning and execution of a
program and supplemental correspondence developed.
Behind all of this, however. is the correspondence that enlists the
participation of many state-wide groups. The General Committee has

122

123

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

~ts own special radi~ and television chairman, always selected from the
industry who, on his own letterhead and over his own signature, sends
out an appeal to all stations for their participation. Copies of the radio
and television booklet are enclosed with his letter.
. . It i~ the further function of the General Committee to solicit the partlc1patlon of large users of metered mail to advertise Public Schools
Week with a special slug. In addition, this past year, the General Committee solicited and obtained the cooperation of the Postmaster General
in the adoption of a cancellation hub in the post offices of: San Francisco, .Oakland, Los Angeles, San Diego, Sacramento and Fresno. The
California Teachers Association generously agreed to share the cost of
the production of the necessary hubs for the cancelling machines. Millions of pieces of mail went out all over the state, to the nation and the
world heralding California's 35th annual Public Schools Week.

Some years ago it was the custom of the Lodges to conflne their
program to events held within Lodge halls. Gradually the practice developed of taking the event to all the people, since the concern and
understanding of the schools was a matter for everyone.
Also the practice has developed of certain lodges in a given area
banding together in their plans for the event. This has proved especially
effective where two or more lodges are making appeals to the same
newspapers, radio and television stations, schoo~ authorities and other
organizations.
It is noteworthy that since this custom has spread throughout the
jurisdiction Public Schools Week has grown and developed in importance until now Governors, the Legislature, Mayors and countless groups
have added their commendation and support. The General Committee
believes that all members of the Fraternity can take a justifiable pride
in the following that has been recruited for this Masonic created and
sponsored event.
·

THE MATTER OF TIMING
Some local committees have expressed a desire to get material earlier
from the General Committee. It has been the custom for the first mailing
piece to go to local chairmen shortly after the first of the year. One
reason for this is that new Masters elected at the close of the year frequently do not get around to the task of naming chairmen for the ensuing year until that time. Another reason is that there is a limit to how
far in advance the General Committee can get its preparatory pieces in
the mail. This is not due to a lack of energy on the part of the General
Committee but the proportions of the task in bringing so many indi~
viduals actually and actively into the event. To accomplish this requires
sustained perseverance.
One answer to this problem is in the local committees themselves.
Each committee plans its program and activities on the foundation of a
rich heritage of the past. Each new committee can be stimulated and
guided by the accomplishments of the committees that have preceded it.
If local committees avail themselves of the background help that is
available to them in their own lodge group they can be well advanced
and prepared for the execution of a full program. Pour months should
be adequate to accomplish this if the job is undertaken with the understanding referred to above.
In reviewing the reports of various lodges one thing stands out clearly
and that is that the best programs are those where one chairman passes
on to next year's chairman a full and detailed account of those things
found most successful in the preceding years.
.

TAKING THE SCHOOLS TO THE PEOPLE
The object of Public Schools Week is to make the schools the common interest and concern of all citizens. Public Schools Week has no
ax to grind. It enters into neither local nor jurisdiction-wide issues. The
event is founded on the principle that if the people are interested in the
.schools all issues fall into their proper perspective.

had been awarded to this event.

Local committees are activated only with the cooperation and participation of their school authorities. It has always been a primary instruction to committees after their organization to first visit their school
authorities and enlist the latter's support and participation. Without this
it is difficult to put on an effective program.
This always has been one of the delicate points in the program and
required tact and an understanding of the relationship of the committee
with the schools. There was always the possibility too of lack of knowledge on the part of some school officials as to the proper sanction behind
the event.
When the California Teachers Association duplicated some of the
program of the General Committee but directed its campaign at the
schools of the state; the chance of misunderstanding was eliminated. The
effect was seen almost instantly in greatly stimulated school participation.
One of the principal pieces of mailing sent out to the teachers was
a manual showing the schools how to take the schools to the people and
how to bring the people to the schools. This same guide also showed
the teachers how to cooperate with the citizens committees sponsoring
Public Schools Week.
All of the association's campaign reached its 72,000 teacher members
either directly or through their schools or teachers' clubs; the latter include more than 500 clubs in the state.
The California Teachers Association also directed a major campaign
to enlist the support of radio and television stations, supplying the latter
with a series of slides to be used in announcing Public Schools Week
and the date. •
The General Committee is deeply grateful to the California Teachers
Association and its members for their help and trust that Public Schools
Week will long enjoy their cooperation.

awards go to Americans and American organizations recognized for
their contributions to better understanding of American freedom through
the things they do. The awards are determined by juries of not less than
thirty American citizens of national distinction one third of whom must

NEWSP APER SUPPOR T
Public Schools Week always enjoys a wide acceptance by the press.
This is part of the heritage that is enjoyed by those working on an event
that has a rich tradition of many years.
There was a time when newspape r editors and others had to be told
what Public Schools Week was and what it endeavore d to accomplish.
Today the problem is largely a matter of bringiiig the anniversa ry to the
editors' attention and supplying such timely, factual data as to give the
news or editorial comment a fresh slant.
The General Committee endeavors to meet this need with a press
book, containing news stories and suggested editorial material. Each
year in preparatio n for this the General Committee does a research
project that endeavors to find those things most important to the schools.
This past year it was the matter of the tragic shortage of teachers and
classrooms. This was due to the influx of the great number of war and
postwar babies now reaching school age and the shifting of populations.
This year's press book included a memorandum of instruction to
chairmen and stories: ( 1 ) announcing the dates, ( 2) on the current
annual shortage of 13,000 accredited teachers, ( 3) on spread of Public
Schools Week to other states, ( 5) symposium of statements by President Eisenhower, Chief Justice Earl Warren and Governor Goodwin
Knight, and ( 5) series of shorts on statement s by Grand Master Frank
Harwell, Jr., Dr. Robert C. Gillingham, president of the California
Teachers Association, Mr. Neil Petree, president California State Chamber of Commerce, C. J. Haggerty, secretary- treasurer California State

RECAPIT ULATION
Public Schools Week has now reached the enviable age of thirtyfive years of observance. It is widely accepted by public officials, the
press, radio and television and by many organization s recruited to the
banner of MasQnry in safeguardin g and furthering the interests of the
Public School.
The slogan-"Th e Public School-An American Heritage" has become a ,p art of the institution that now is dedicated in the calendars of
many groups and organization s as "Public Schools Week."
Public Schools Week has won national recognition in the award of
the Freedoms Foundation George Washington gold medal. It has been
adopted by other states as an important activity of Masonry.
Now that 72,000 classroom teachers in California have been definitely joined in the undertaking through the California Teachers Association
there can be no question as to how thoroughly and widespread has been
the adoption of this annual program.
All of the foregoing is a challenge to Masonry. It is only heing realistic to say that the wider the acclaim given this event the more of a
l'esponsibility it becomes to see that Public Schools Week grows in importance with each passing year. That is the price that is paid for success.
The General Committee hopes that this report in itself will help
reveal the scope and the extent of the obligation Pu~lic Schools Week

130

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

imposes. That all Masters will make the selection of their chairmen for
this event an early obligation. That they be chosen for their proven
capacity to furnish leadership for the diverse groups to be brought into
the program.
Public Schools Week traditionally falls on the week of the fourth
Monday in April, which in 1955 would be April 25th-30th. This information has been transmitted to the school people throughout the state.
A chairman named by the first of the year with the records of past programs available to him should be able to produce an outstanding observance.
Experience has proved that there is definite merit in a campaign
bound in definite time limits. Enthusiasm and interest can be maintained
at an effective pitch only for a certain period, the actual time required
to get the job done. Committeemen and others recognizing the urgency
in getting the job done in time can be stimulated to greater effort. Too
much time frequently develops procrastination in getting things accomplished and proves a definite slowing influence on the entire project.
In closing, the important factor in an effective Public Schools Week
program is the local chairman. An enthusiastic, resourceful chairman
will surround himself with a strong, capable committee. He will acquaint
himself with the procedures of the past that ·have brought worthwhile
results. He will make definite and specific assignments to those working
with him and he will see that these are carried out as planned.
All of this is reflected in the more than 600 reports throughout the
jurisdiction now at ·hand and which the General Committee has reviewed.
To thumb these pages and study the exhibits is to feel a deep sense
of respect for the mobilized strength of Masonry, directed at protecting
and helping the Public School, an institution as American as our flag.

PROCLAMATION OF THE GRAND MASTER
M.W. FRANK HARWELL, . }R.

To the Masters, Wardens and Brethren of California:
The struggle of man for freedom and the dignity that adorns freedom is an old story but one that has attained increasing importance in
these present years of uncertainties.
Perhaps never before has man lived in a world of such opposites
where he has to take his stand for freedom as against slavery; integrity
as against degradation; Christian brotherliness as opposed to primitive
brutality.
Sometimes we see as through a glass darkly but the image is becoming more and more clearly revealed. The struggle now is for the minds
of men. Certainly we need strong bodies, spiritual growth and stout
courage. But we also need clean-cut concepts of the way of life of free
men.
Our forefathers in their prophetic wisdom provided the instrumentality for all of this in the public school which today assumes increasing
importance as we look to our youth to take up the burden of the struggle
which we must soon pass on to them.
Masonry can well take pride in its devotion to the principle of free
schools-free from bigotry and falsehood as we prepare our own inspired thirty-fifth annual Public Schools Week.
I. therefore, proclaim and direct:
That all Lodges in California observe Public Schools Week ·April
26th through May 1st, 1954;
That no meetings be held during that week except stated meetings
that fall therein and meetings for Public Schools Week observance;
That this proclamation be read at each stated meeting prior to April
26th, 1954.
Dated at San Francisco January 4th, 1954.

PROCLAMATION OF YORK RITE BODIES
Dear Companions and Sir Knights:
WILLIAM R. MARKLE, Grand High Priest
JOSEPH A. GARRY, Grand Master
JOHN R. MOORE, Grand Commander
For more than a generation the Grand Lodge of Masons in California has sponsored an annual stock-taking of our school system
through the medium of Public Schools Week.
The 35th annual observance of this event by direction of Grand
Master Frank Harwell, Jr., will be held April 26th through May 1, 1954.
Our forefathers wisely foresaw the importance of education to the
successful functioning of a government by law. Nothing else is quite so
American as the Public School.
It has been said that the real battleground of freedom is in the minds
of men. The issue is: shall the minds of men remain free or shall they
become enslaved? So long as youth is adequately prepared through free
public schools for the responsibility of citizenship, there can 1be no question of the outcome.
The York Rite Bodies have always cooperated with the Grand
Lodge in its sponsorship of this worthy event. Therefore, we ask the
High Priests, the Illustrious Masters and the Commanders to urge visits
to one or more local schools during the Public Schools Week Period.

To All Officers, California Jurisdiction:
RE: 35TH ANNUAL PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK
The 35th Annual Public Schools Week will be held April 26 through
May 1, 1954.
For the past thirty-five years, Public Schools Week has been a
means in California of calling attention annually to the functions and
needs of our public schools. The main goal is to get the public to visit
the schools and see what is going on. We are interested in making sure,
among other things, that the American public schools remain sanctuaries
of religious freedom-required by law to ·be free from sectarian control
-where no person or church may dictate what the children must believe
in matters of religion. The subject of church selection and dogma is left
to the ·home, the individual, the church, and the Sunday School. with
free choice from the diversity of religious creeds and practices guaranteed and given to us under our constitutional form of government.
Accordingly, is it my request that we support the observance this
year and plan to ·participate. It is a Masonic-sponsored event. It is hoped
that, among other things, our Scottish Rite members will endeavor to
visit one or more schools in their communities during the week.
Please publicize the above through such outlets as may be available
to you.

WHEREAS, the week commencing MONDAY, APRIL 26th,

decree that there be no meetings, Ceremonials, Entertainments or Functions of any nature held under the auspices of any Pyramid during the
week commencing APRIL 26th, 1954 to MAY 1, 1954, and that every
Sciot co-operate with his Masonic Lodge by personal attendance at any
meeting arranged ·by the Committee on Public Schools Week. This is
in accordance with the principles, aims and objects of the Ancient Egyptian Order of Sciots, to further the interests of every child, to assure
them of a sane, sound education, fitting the individual for a life of self
ttspecting, self supporting, law abiding citizenship. Officers elective and
appointive are asked to carry out the ·provisions of the above edict, and

STATEMENT OF GOVERNOR OF HAWAII
HON. SAMUEL WILDER KING
{Note: the dates for the observance of Public Schools Week were
earlier in 1954 than those in California.)
It is a pleasure for me to express my support of the observance of
Public Schools Week, starting February 22.
Our public schools occupy an important place in the history of our
country. They have undergone numerous trials and tribulations, and
have been under attack on occasions. Having withstood these difficulties,
the public schools stand today as one of the greatest bulwarks of our
free society.
I commend the Masonic Order for its continued sponsorship of
Public Schools Week. The program which the Masonic Order is arranging on the evening of February 25, 1954, at Lincoln Elementary School
will help to promote greater understanding of our public schools.
It is incumbent upon citizens of every community to maintain their
active interest in public education, in order that the public schools can
be of even greater value to our society. The annual observance of
Public Schools Week affords the opportunity each year for our citizens
to acquaint themselves with the principles upon which the public schools
system is founded.
As an expression of my own interest on behalf of free public education, I requested the Commissioners of Public Instruction to abolish the
kindergarten fees of $3.00 a month for each pre-school child, and to
eliminate the book rental charges.
As of December 1, 1953, the Commissioners of Public Instruction
have abolished the kindergarten fees and are now making plans to
eliminate book rentals at the start of the next school year.

to light. These have been filed for future action but a great deal more
needs to be done which will involve considerable follow-up work over a
period of time-if indeed the work can ever be completely concluded.
Such mistakes as have occurred were the result of honest error and entirely unintenional. Most of the omissions concerned material undisclosed at the time of publication and which came to our attention after
the books were puiblished. Because of the great volume of historical
matter which was assembled by the committee, some of it had to be omitted in the interest of consolidation for economy's sake alone but which
rightfully belonged in the printed history. There remains a considerable
amount of this unused material in the files which could be worked up and
published in pamphlet form from time to time.
The publication of the books seems to have awakened what was a
latent and ·possibly an apathetic interest in the history of our craft in
California. So much so, that a number of incidents of historical value
have come to our attention which your committee has begun to pursue
and which, when fully investigated will be written up and filed for future
use. One of these was the ill-fated and tragic Henry Crabb expedition
into the State of Sonora, in Mexico, in 1857. The purpose of the expedition was to colonize Sonora and to exert pressure for an honest and
democratic government of the department. The leader, Henry· Crabb,
was a Mason, as were many of the 78 members of his party. An undetermined number of them were members of this jurisdiction including
the first Worshipful Master of Martinez Lodge No. 41-Brother Ro bert
N. Wood, and the Marshal of San Jose Lodge No. 10, Brother F. S.
McKinney. All 78, including these and the leader, Henry Crabb, were
forced -to surrender to the Mexican Army at Caborca, Sonora, Mexico,
and were tied up, marched out in batches facing an adobe wall outside
the local cemetery, and shot to death in the back. Their bodies lay unburied where they fell for days to be eaten by dogs, hogs, and such wild
animals as were attracted and the ·bones finally buried in a common grave
without benefit of ceremony. Your committee learned of this incident
only as the books were going to press and touched upon it lightly in the
chapter on Martinez Lodge. There was insufficient time to secure all of
the details and in fact those given here came to light only this past May.
There still remains much more to be done to assemble the complete story.
Past Grand Master James Black Gist passed away on April 25, 1954
and was buried on April 28, 1954 in Space #1. Lot 1037, Whispering
Pines Section, Forest Lawn Memorial Park, Glendale, California.
Past Grand Master, William B. Ogden, passed away on Septem!ber
1954 and was buried on September 15, 1954 in grave "H" plot 164 Olive
section 10, Glen Haven Memorial Park, San Fernando, California.

Lodges, determine the facts and write up such stories for future use.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC 1-llSTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report:
During the past year the committee has engaged in a number of
projects concerning the contemporary history of this jurisdiction. In
addition to considerable correspondence between the members of the
committee and your chairman, a number of intra-committee conferences
have been held, centennial celebrations attended, and a general meeting
of the entire committee during the spring which was attended by all
members with the exception of one who lives in the southern part of
the state. After careful and considered discussion, involving future plans
and activities of the committee, a course of action was unanimously
adopted, to be made a part of this report, for recommendation to and
consideration by this Grand Lodge.
An effective history committee, if it he more than a mere name, should
have the responsibility of collecting and assembling in its proper order
and form information regarding events and personalities which transpire from day to day. Such information-gathering requires the services
of a number of trained, sincere, diligent, ardent and dependable workers.
preferably spread over the jurisdiction in order to secure adequate ~ov­
erage. Information so gathered should be catalogued and filed against
the day when it can 1b e made available for editing and publishing as a
part of the history of this Grand Jurisdiction. This your committee has
been attempting to do and since the publication in 1950 of "100 Years
of Freemasonry in California," considerable material has already found
.
its way into the files.
Since 1950, when this jurisdiction celebrated its 1OOth anniversary,
a number of centennial celebrations have been held. As the years pass
from now on to the end of time there will continue to be yearly centennial celebrations among the constituent Lodges. Your history committee
has been of considerable assistance to most of these Lodges in preparing
the historical data for their celebrations and of some small measure of
service to the Grand Officers also along these same lines. Demands now
on file as well as planned future celebrations indicate the need for a
continuing program of service to these Lodges which your committee
.
plans to undertake.

They must be real Masons to put in the time and effort required in
starting a new lodge, and we feel that the interests of Masonry are
advanced in having such men active in its service.
The number being so large we feel that it would take too much of
Grand Lodge time and too many printed pages in the proceedings to
give you a briefing on each lode separately, though there is much of
interest that could be said. Therefore, we report to you that all lodges

REPORT ON FOREST LODGE NO. 66
At last year's Communication, your Committee on Charters had referred to it that portion of Grand Master Warren's message concerning
Forest Lodge No. 66 at Allegheny which is in the northern part of the
Mother Lode country. This dealt with the failure of Forest Lodge to
comply with certain provisions of our law. On the recommendation of
your Committe~. Grand Lodge granted a year's grace in order that the
promised efforts at revitalization or consolidation might be attempted.
While the Lodge has not complied with all legal requirements, we
are pleased to report that an earnest and sincere endeavor has been made
to perpetuate the existence of this 100 year old Lodge. The meeting day
has been changed to .Saturday and we are informed that five meetings
have been held with a quorum present, not an easy task where only
three members live in this isolated and remote mining camp.
Your Committee strongly urges the officers and members of Forest
Lodge to effect a consolidation with one of the other Lodges in the high
Sierras to the end that the century-old continuity of this Lodge will not
be ended, and that Masonry may be strengthened in this area of small
and historic Lodges. Their inspector, Worshipful Edward Farley, concurs in this recommendation.
We therefore recommend that Forest Lodge No. 66 be granted a
further period not to exceed one year in order that this Lodge may ensure its continuance through fulfilling all the requirements of the law, or
effecting a consolidation with another Lodge, or surrendering its Charter.
Adopted.

The resolution presented to this Grand Lodge by California Lodge
No. 1 requesting the sum not to exceed $350.00 for the purpose of paying the cost of a fitting monument over the grave of our first Grand
Master, Jonathan Drake Stevenson, was referred to this committee for
consideration.
The Committee on Finance is sympathetic with the request of California Lodge No. 1. and is including in its recommended appropriation.
the sum of $350.00 to be used as requested.
There has been referred to this Committee. that portion of the Grand
Master's message wherein he recommended that Past Grand Master
Leslie E. Wood be sent to the Hawaiian Islands. He further reported
that in view of some of the problems involving the Lodges in the Islands.
as Chairman of the Policy and General Purposes Committee, it was the
Grand Master's considered judgment that much good could be gained
by extending this courtesy to Past Grand Master Leslie E. Wood. he
having been one of the Grand Masters who was deprived of this pleasure as a result of the Second World War.
Your Committee on Finance feels that to a certain extent this is a
matter to be determined by the incoming Grand Master and that if in
his judgment such a trip is desirable or essential a sufficient amount
should be appropriated from the surplus to cover the cost thereof.
MASONIC HOMES
A review of the report of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes followed by consultation with them as to the needs for the coming year
indicate that a renewal of the per capita tax of 50c together with other
anticipated income will be sufficient to properly maintain our Homes
for the ensuing year. We. therefore. propose the following resolution
and move its adoption:
RESOLVED: That the sum of 50c per capita be levied for
the fiscal year. 1955-56. the proceeds to be paid to the Trustees
of the Masonic Homes.

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON PUBLICATI ONS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
As an introduction to the presentation of the activities, recommenda..
tions and conclusions of this committee, we believe that it will be proper
for Grand Lodge to know certain facts concerning the committee.
Every member of the committee sat in two of the four meetings of
the committee held during the year. Four members were present at all
meetings. All of the members of the committee have been continually
informed of the work being done by the other members. Each action of
the committee, each recommendation of the committee and each conclusion reached and presented to you here has been discussed and debated
within the committee and has been unanimously adopted. This has been
a working committee in the real sense of the word and, as Chairman, I
wish to thank the members who have devoted their time, energies and
talents to a difficult task. I wish also to express to our Grand Master
the sincere appreciation of each member of the committee for the many
hours of consultation which he, busy as he is, gave to us and to this
problem. His devotion to duty marks him as a Master among our
Grand Masters.
This committee was entrusted by our Grand Master with a solemn
responsibility to this Grand Lodge. Your predecessor Masters and
Wardens, as the representatives of the Lodges of this jurisdiction, wrote
into the law ( let it be noted, by a five-sixths vote) a paragraph to section
127 of our Ordinances which, in substance, said to all Masons in California "you may not advertise your business or profession in any
publication or medium purporting to be Masonic in name or characternor may you solicit advertising in such a publication without the express
sanction of this Grand Lodge."
This legislation was enacted for two purposes: First, to remove the
stain of commercialism from Masonic activity, and second, to protect
the gullible and unwary from the depredation of various racketeering
publishers who were using the name, emblems and symbols of Masonry
as bait to fleece the public and members of the Craft as well.
Whether non-sanctioned publications still existed was not deAnitely
known at the start of this year. Strong suspicion remained that they
would not give up the rich repast which they had enjoyed. They had
fed upon the body of Masonry and also upon its friends among the
public at large. They had used the name of Masonry to obtain donated

PUBLICATIONS OPERATING UNDER SANCTION

Certain publications had, however, been among those which various
Grand Masters had granted sanction for Masons to solicit advertising
for or place advertising in and as of the appointment of this committee,
the following sanctions were outstanding:
1. Masonic News, Huntington Park, California, Marguerite Pray,
Publisher-Ro bert Mero, member Bell Lodge No. 483, advertising manager.
2. Seaboard Mason and Eastern Star, Long Beach, California,
Charles G. de Coudries, member Palos Verdes Lodge No. 389,
publisher.
3. Square and Compass, Lomita, California, Gordon Chambers,
member Lomita Lodge No. 644, publisher.
4. Southern California Masonic Journal, Ontario, California, Henry
C. Engler, member Ontario Lodge No. 301, publisher.
5. Masonic Herald, Anaheim, California, Leo J. Friis, member Anaheim Lodge No. 207, publisher.
6. Southern California Shriner and Bay Area Mason, Santa Monica,
California, Calvin Carey, publisher, member Southern California
Lodge No. 278.
7. Kern County Masonry and Eastern Star, Bakersfield, California,
Mike S. Oldershaw, member Bakersfield Lodge No. 224, publisher.
8. San Luis Obispo County Mason and Eastern Star, San Luis
Obispo, Marcus L. Waltz, member San Simeon Lodge No. 196,
· publisher.
9. Channel Counties Mason and Eastern Star, Santa Barbara, California, Cecil L. Loomis, member Magnolia Lodge No. 242, publisher.
10. The Shriner, Santa Barbara, California, Cecil L. Loomis, member
Magnolia Lodge No. 242, prospective publisher. (This sanction
had ·been granted but no issues had been printed.)
The publications operating under sanction had applied thru previous
· committees and sanction had been granted Masons to advertise therein,
based upon certain statements and promises made by the publishers as
to the ethical conduct of their business, both as to the solicitation of
advertising and as to their relationship with Lodges whose Trestle
Boards they might carry.
Among other promises entered into within the previous year, were
the following:

150

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

1. That no use would be made of any Lodge roster or official mem#
bership list.
2. That no money would be solicited or received from any Lodge for
subscriptions or otherwise and that no representation would be made to
Masons that it was their duty to subscribe or advertise.
3. That advertising would not be solicited by anyone not a member
of a California lodge and never upon a commission basis or by telephone.
4. That no representation would be made that the publication was
representative of Grand Lodge or of any constituent Lodge or that any
benefit, financial or otherwise, would accrue to Masonry in general,
directly or indirectly, thru its advertising revenues.
PHASES OF PROBLEM

The publication problem may, therefore, be divided into two phases,
and questions arise as to each1. As to so#called sanctioned publications: Are the agreements
entered into by the .publishers being honored?
2. As to so--called non#sanctioned publications: Do they still exist?
How do they operate? Who operates them? Are they operated by
Masons? If operated by non-Masons, how best can we fulfill our
responsibility as a Grand Lodge in stamping out this evil?
These were the questions propounded to the committee by your
Grand Master. The committee was composed of members of Grand
Lodge who had not ·been involved in any previous disscussions of the
problem and who were not associated with any local situation which
might tend to color their viewpoint. The committee was, therefore, free
from any preconceived ideas as to either the duties of the committee or
the solution of the problem. Most of the members had not seen more
than one or two of the publications in question.
Your Grand Master established two fundamental ground rules:
( 1 ) GET THE FACTS, and
( 2) LET THE CHIPS FALL WHERE THEY MAY.
SURVEY OF ADVERTISERS IN SANCTION ED PUBLICATI ONS

To this end, at its initial meeting held in Los Angeles on January 10,
1954, the committee determined that a survey of advertisers in "sane#
tioned" publications should be made. The letter to advertisers and
questionnaire, (Exhibits A and B), were therefore, drawn by the com#
mittee acting as a whole and were sent to each of the advertisers ap#
pearing in the December 1953 or other latest issue of each sanctioned
·
publication.
The returns from advertisers in a particular publication were direct#
ed to one of the members of your committee and tabulated by that
member, so that each member received and tabulated an approximate
equal number of answers. Replies received from Masons and those
received from non#Masons were separately compiled, and we have these
on file.
