Trial Record No. 1374
To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge of California:

The accused R. W . R. was on the 3rd day of Februar y, 1954, after
notice duly given, expelled by South Gate Lodge No. 320 F. & A. M.
from all of the rights and privileges of Masonr y by reason of the con..
viction of a crime classified as a felony, to wit: the crime of Infliction
of Trauma tic Injury upon Wife of Accused, and was imprisoned therefor.
The expulsion of the accused has been approved by your Committee

217

in its Omnibus Report, which said report has been approved by Grand
Lodge at this communication.
On July 15, 1954, the accused R. W.R. filed with South Gate Lodge
No. 320 F. & A. M. a petition for restoration to the rights and privileges
of Masonry. The Lodge at its stated meeting 'held on September 1. 1954,
after notice duly given, voted unanimously to petition Grand Lodge to
restore R. W. R. under the provisions of Section 347 of Ross Digest.
Section 327 of ordinances provides for review of trial records by
Grand Lodge. In Section 916 of Ross Digest Section 327 was construed
and discussed. It is necessary in all cases that the Trial Record be reviewed by Grand Lodge and action taken thereon. Since in this case
the Trial Record was not confirmed by Grand Lodge until Octobe r 11.
1954, it is the opinion of your Committee that the petition of South Gate
Lodge No. 320 F. & A. M. is premature.
In addition, the petition of R. W. R. to the Lodge does not show
what he has done to rehabilitate himself after his conviction and that he
completely atoned for his acts.
For the foregoing reasons it is the opinion o'f your Committee that
the petition of South Gate Lodge No. 320 F. & A. M. be denied without
prejudice, and recommends the adoption of the following resolution:
RESOL VED: That the petition of South Gate Lodge No. 320 F.
& A. M. in Trial Record No. 1374 for restoration of R. W. R. to the
rights and privileges of Masonr y be and the same is hereby denied,
without prejudice.
Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1382
To the Most ?Vorshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1382, reports as follows:
Accused V . W ., a member of Blackmer Lodge No. 442, was charged
with several specifications involving possession of and addiction to
narcotics.
He was tried and found guilty of all specifications and of unmasonic
conduct and penalty was fixed by expelling him from all rights and privileges of masonry. With this your committee is in full agreement.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

218

However, the committee feels compelled to comment upon the state
of the trial record which indicates the Trial Commission met on a certain
date for which a meeting was called, and adjourn ed to a later date, but
in the meantime at the express direction of the Grand Master the action
of trial procedure was deferre d until a trial master could be designa ted
to take the place of the Master who was disqualified. Pursuan t to this
direction the Trial Commissioners. accused, accuser and Master were
advised not to appear on the date specified and that a new date would
be set as soon as a Trial Master could be appoint ed. This was done in
due time and the trial took place.
Because of the express direction on the part of the Grand Master,
your committee feels this matter should be considered as an exception
to Section 983 of Ross Digest.
Therefo re, your committee recommends the following resolution and
moves its adoption:
RESOL VED: That the Trial Commissions did have jurisdiction and
that their finding in Trial Record No. 1382 that V. W. is guilty of the
specification and of unmasonic conduct be and it is hereby affirmed and
approved; and that by action of Grand Lodge the said V. W. be expelled
from all rights and privileges of Masonr y.
Adopte d.

Trial Record No. 1384
To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge of California:
This trial record involves one J. C. C.. Jr.. a member of East San
Diego Lodge No. 561.
In court the accused plead guilty to two different counts of grand
theft, was fined $2,000 and put on 5 years probation. In the masonic
trial he was charged with two specifications: ( 1 ) that of stealing a compressor of the value of $3.500, and ( 2) theft of a table saw of the value
of $1,000.
He was present and testified at the masonic trial. The Trial Commission found him guilty of both specifications and unmasonic conduct
fixing the penalty at suspension.
Under the circumstances and in keeping with Grand Lodge precedents of expelling a member in similar cases, your Committee offers the
following resolution.
RESOL VED: That the Trial Commission's finding that J.C. C., Jr.,
is guilty of unmasonic conduct be affirmed. but that the penalty therefor e
be fixed by Grand Lodge at expulsion.
Adopte d.

Trial Record No. 1388
To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge of California:
The accused R. N. K., a member of Hollyw ood Lodge No. 355, was

convicted in the Superio r Court of Los Angele s County of violations
of several sections of the narcotics laws of Californ ia, in that he forged
and altered a prescription for a narcotic to wit: demerol, and also was
convicted of the crime of burglar y, a felony, by wilfully entering a store
and building with intent to commit theft. Accused was granted probation by the court for a period of five years, with one year of this time
to be served in the County Jail. He actually served seven months on the
County Road Camp. He was also ordered to make restitution to the
owner of the store for damage s in the sum of $6.000.
Upon specifications based on the foregoing facts he was charged
with unmasonic conduct, tried and found guilty of the specifications,
but not guilty of unmasonic conduct.
Your Committee feels that the crimes of which he was found guilty
by the Trial Commission involved moral turpitud e.
Under the circumstances we are of the opinion that the finding of
"not guilty of unmasonic conduc t" is unwarr anted and should be set
aside, and that Grand Lodge should supply a finding of "guilty of unmasonic conduct " and that the penalty should be fixed at expulsion.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOL VED: That the Trial Commission's finding in Trial Record
No. 1388 that R. N. K. is guilty of the specifications ·be approve d and
affirmed; that by action of this Grand Lodge the accused be adjudge d
guilty of unmasonic conduc t and that he be and is hereby expelled from
all rights and privileges of Masonr y.
Adopte d.

standing alone, might not be sufficient for a finding of guilt herein. But
it appears that accused actually knew that in Masonry he would be
barred from membership if he told of his felony convictions and his
answer to the question was therefore wilfully false.
The members who advised him to conceal these facts were also to
blame, but accused cannot excuse himself because of their wrong.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That the expulsion of B. H. E. M. by Silver Gate
Lodge No. 296 be approved and affirmed.
Adopted.

sonic offense; it is the operation of a bar or being a bar-tender that is
the offense and this is not charged.
El Sereno Lodge was advised to amend these charges to make them
express some Masonic offense or offenses, but did not do so.
The record is very poor. We do not have the full record of the meeting at which commissioners were elected. Service on accused was probably sufficient, although the record on that point is not clear.
At the trial no legal evidence whatever was produced except possibly the copy of the application of accused for a liquor license in Colorado. The rest consisted of unsworn letters, newspaper articles, etc. All
of these are hearsay evidence only. A proper deposition, sworn to by
some proper witness in Colorado, could have proved the necessary facts
of this case in a few typewritten pages, but we have no such evidence in
the file.
The able trial master continued the trial once to enable the Lodge
to get some real evidence. HO'Wever, on the date set by the trial master
the latter was out of the state and apparently the matter was continued
another week, although the record does not show it. At the final meeting
the trial master was still absent and the commission proceeded without
him, took some further evidence and voted, finding accused guilty of the
fourth specification and of unmasonic conduct and ordered him expelled.
No record is made of the vote on the first three specifications.
Although there is every indication that this Entered Apprentice
Mason, who has been properly stopped from advancement, should be
expelled, we cannot recommend it on a poor record like we have here.
The charges are not properly drawn and the evidence was completely
illegal and inadmissible and the procedure was faulty "in many respects.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That the expulsion of S. G. F. by El Sereno Lodge
No. 588 be reversed and set aside and the matter returned to the Lodge
for the filing of amended charges as to being in the saloon business or
acting as a bar-keeper and for a new trial on such charges.
Adopted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
S. G. F., the accused, was elected to take the Degrees in El Sereno
Lodge No. 588 in 1952, and received the Entered Apprentice Degree.
He then moved to Colorado and later asked that he be permitted to take
the remaining Degrees there. Correspondence with Masonic officials in
Colorado led to the information that accused was operating a place
where liquor was sold in violation of Colorado Masonic law and that

was stopped from such advancement. However, he was still an Entered
Apprentice of the Lodge and the Grand Master advised the Lodge to
proceed to try him.
Charges were filed in several specifications:
( 1 ) That he had participated in a gun-shooting affair in which one
man was killed and in which accused was wounded.
( 2) That he "threw a punch. at a man which missed and struck the
man's wife."
( 3) That he had participated in a gambling disagreement in which
ill-feeling was generated. ·
( i ) That he had a liquor license for serving by the drink issued to
him in Colorado.
As drawn, none of these specifications state Masonic offenses. It is
not shown that accused was in any way to blame in the gun-shooting
affair, but it appears he was one of the victims.
It is not shown that the throwing of the punch which hit the intended
recipient's wife was wrongful. It may have been in self-defense, and
the correspondence in the file so indicates.
It is not shown that the gambling disagreement involves any wrongful action by accused.

Trial Record No. 1400
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to which was referred trial record No. 1iOO, reports
as follows:
The accused, W. J. L. was charged with unmasonic conduct in that
he stole property of his employer of the value of $236.00. Although not
served with process in accordance with our Law he appeared at the time
of trail and testified on his own behalf.
The evidence is sufficient to support findings of guilty of the specification of unmasonic conduct. However, the record in this respect reads
as follows:

222

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

"After sufficient consultation and deliberation, a vote for guilty or
not guilty was taken by ballot and the ballot was seven ( 7) guilty and
none ( 0) not guilty. The Commissioners then proceeded to vote by
ballot, upon the sentence. The Master submitted to the Commissioners
the question-Shal l the accused be expelled? The ballot on such question resulted in six ( 6) aye, and one ( 1 ) no." (End of quote.)
It will be noted that in fact no separate ballots were taken on the

However, in this matter, your committee is of the opinion that this
error was not prejudicial to the accused.
We therefore present the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That in Trial Record No. 1400, a finding of guilt
of the specification and of unmasonic conduct be supplied by action of
this Grand Lodge; that the penalty be fixed at expulsion, and that the
action of The Gardens Lodge No. 621, in expelling W. J. L. from all the
rights and privileges of Masonry be and the same hereby is ratified, confirmed and approved.
Adopted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

G. M. W .• a member of Claremont Lodge No. 436, was a constable

Trial Record No. 1405
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1405 reports as follows:
Accused, A.G. H., a member of Euclid Lodge No. 519, was charged
with unmasonic conduct in three specifications: first, that accused hit a
person (while driving an automobiie) and did not stop to render aid or
give his name; second, that he was convicted in the Superior Court for

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

223

violation of Section 480 of the Vehicle Code of California; and third,
that he was imprisoned in the County Jail for the term of 60 days as a
condition of a three year probation period. The first specification alone
states the offense.
The accused appeared at the trial and testified that he ran over a
man and killed him; that he lost control of his faculties and drove away
from the scene of the accident, subsequently realized that he had done
wrong; that the evidence showed that the man he had killed was drunk
and walking in the middle of the road; that he realized that he had done
wrong in not stopping at the scene of the accident.
He was found guilty of specification one, "Hit-run," not guilty of
specifications two and three, and not guilty of unmasonic conduct.
The trial commissioners correctly found him guilty of the first specification. Your Committee feels that the trial commissioners erred in finding him not guilty of unmasonic conduct. The accused pleaded guilty
in the Criminal Court. He admitted he was wrong in leaving. the scene
of the accident. There must have been extenuating circumstances because
the Criminal Court gave him a light sentence when he served 60 days in
an honor camp for the offense involved. Nevertheless he should have
been found guilty of unmasonic conduct and a "light" Masonic penalty
assessed.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move for its adoption:
RESOLVED: That the Trial Commission's finding in Trial Record
No. 1405, that A. G. H. is guilty of specification one be approved and
affirmed; that the.finding that he is not guilty of unmasonic conduct be
disapproved and a finding of guilty be supplied: and that the penalty be
and it is hereby fixed at reprimand.
Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1406
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1406 reports as follows:
Accused F. C. L., a member of Signal Lodge No. 543, was charged
with unmasonic conduct in three specifications: first, that accused knowingly, wilfully and unlawfully sold or issued shares of stock of "X"
Company, a Nevada Corporation, without a permit from the Commissioner of Corporations of California; second, that he failed to pay du~
obedience to the laws under whose protection he lives by selling shares
in said corporation contrary to the Corporate Securities Act of Califor~
nia and which would constitute a felony: and third, that he did commercialize on Masonry by using a roster or list of Masons as a "sucker"
list of prospects for the sale of shares in said venture.
The accused appeared at the trial and was represented by an attor-

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

224

ney. A certified copy of the judgment of conviction in the Superior Court
on his plea of guilty was introduced for violation of the Corpor ate
Securities Act. He was fined $500.00, put on 5 years probation and
ordered to pay three-fo urths of the total amount of restitution resulting
from the illegal sale of stock.
The accused testified that he had personally invested a large amount
of funds in the venture, all of which was lost due to the untimely death
and drunkenness of other principals: that he had an opinion from an
attorney that the sale of stock in Nevada through a power of attorne y
would not violate California law and subsequently the attorne y reversed
his position and wrote a letter that sale of stock was not legal: that
accused had no intention of violating the Corpor ate Securities Act and
did not use his Masonic connections whatsoever for the sale of stock,
that all sales were made to investors who voluntarily wished to invest
and no pressure was used on them.
The trial commissioners found the accused guilty of the first and
second specifications and not guilty of the third: guilty of unmasonic
conduct and penalty fixed at expulsion. The matter is now before us on
a written appeal by the accused claiming that the evidence is insufficient
to sustain the judgment: that the specifications are incomplete and do
not state sufficient facts to constitute grounds for expulsion: that additional evidence has been procured by the accused: that a misunderstanding was prevalent among the Commissioners at the time that they made
their decision.
We can dispose of the contention that there was a misunderstanding
among the Commissioners because there is no evidence thereof whatso ever. The brief filed hy the accused in support of the appeal does not
mention this point or present any evidence. In support of the contention
that the specifications are incomplete it is claimed that the specifications
neglect to set forth that the accused was convicted of a felony and his
sentence for such offense. Such matter is improper in a specification and
the specifications upon which the accused was expelled are sufficient.
The additional evidence, consisting of powers of attorne y to purchase
stock in Nevada and a financial breakdown of the money collected and
spent by the corporation is m~rely c~mulative. The evi.dence a~d~ced at
the trial was sufficient to sustain the 1udgment of the trial comnuss1oners,
particularly in view of the accused's plea of guilty in the criminal court.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move for its adoption:
RESOL VED: That the Trial Commissioners' finding in Trial Record No. 1406, that F. C. L. be expelled be and the same is hereby approved and confirmed.
Adopted.

REPORT OF COMMIT TEE ON NECROLO GY
Life is a continuous succession of joys and sorrows. The convening
of the Grand Lodge is a joyous occasion for again we contact those from
whom we have been separated for a time. It also is a sad occasion for
we seek in vain for those whom we have been closely associated with
over the years, and the realization gradually creeps upon us that never
again will we see their smiling faces nor grasp their hands in the salutation of friendship. Therefore it is fitting and proper that we pause in
our deliberations to pay our respects to, and express our love for, those
members who have during the past year been called to the Grand Lodge
a.hove.
Since the 1953 Communication 249 members of the Grand Lodge
Body have crossed into the great unknown and, according to our belief
and our faith. now reside in our Father's house under the protection of
His everlasting arms.
The vast area of California, over which spreads the Masonic Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge. makes it impossible for any one of us to
have known each of our deceased brethren. But it is doubtful indeed
if there is a single one present who has not during the past year stood
beside the bier of one or more of our dead and there shed his tears at the
loss of a good man, a dear friend, and an ardent Mason.
The devoted interest of our deceased brethren to the wellbeing of
our Fraternity is manifested by the fact that 153 had been members
between 25 and 50 years and 40 had been members for over half a
century.
The death toll was heaviest in Pacific Lodge No. 136 of San Francisco and West Gate Lodge No. 335 of Los Angeles, each having lost
four Past Masters. Twelve lodges lost three each, 47 lodges lost two

occupancy of the Oriental Chair he served two years as Junior Steward,
twelve years as Senior Steward, twelve years as Senior Deacon, and two
years as Senior Warden. An unusual record, a remarkable man.
Brother Kennedy held the banner of Masonry high and we are proud
to list his name as one of our honored dead.
We mourn the passing of our brethren but we do not question God's
wisdom nor his right to call them. We give the Great Light our deepest
thanks that they were with us and of us and they shall ever remain
beautiful thoughts in our garden of memory. The poet has beautifully
expressed it:
"To a Beautiful Garden these friends have gone
To the land of perfect rest.
Their work is done. and the setting sun
Has sealed their life's long quest.
They have left this earthly garden
For a home beyond the sea,
Though they have gone, they still live on
In our Gafden of Memory."

ated from Lake Forest College in 1910. Soon afterward he moved to
San Diego to establish his permanent home.
In 1913 he married Miss Daisy Bentley. a graduate of Northwestern
University. His charming and gracious wife, three lovely daughters,
two fine sons and nine splendid grandchildren survive him.
Shortly after his arrival in California, Brother Morrison was em ..
ployed by the First National Bank of San Diego. To talents of no
ordinary measure he added an infinite capacity for intensive work.
While others slumbered, he toiled; earnest and careful preparation for
his tasks was habitual. With characteristic skill and devotion to duty
he earned promotion after promotion and at the time of his death he was
Vice President of the bank and a member of its Board of Directors.
In the business world his judgment was highly respected. He was
fearless but fair in the discharge of his duties, gave everyone a courteous
and impartial hearing, was always open to conviction but firm in his
judgments when formed.
He gave unstintingly of his time in the furtherance of worthy public
enterprises and always sought to promote the welfare of his fellow men.
He was a virile citizen who ever stood courageously for decency and
right. His voice was always heard on the side of civic virtue. He was
active for many years in the affairs of the First Methodist Church.
Brother Morrison will long be remembered here because of his kindly
disposition, his sincere friendships and those sterling qualities that made
him a great Mason. For him, Masonry was a tool to be used for the
service of mankind and he performed that service with distinction in all
the Masonic Bodies.
Of his Masonic career. one of his San Diego brethren has appropriately said: "His activities ... covered a period of more than 40 years.
He was made a Master Mason in Pontiac Lodge No. 294 on February
23, 1911, demitted to San Diego Lodge No. 35 in 1921, and served as
Worshipful Master in 1924. He shortly afterward became active in
Grand Lodge affairs. After service as Grand Standard Bearer, as a
member of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and of
Finance, he was chosen, in 1940, to entered the Grand Lodge 'line,"
and in 1943 was elected and served with distinction as Grand Master
of Masons in California-the first and only Grand Master from San
Diego. He has since been chairman of the important Grand Lodge
Finance Committee.
He was coroneted as a Mason of the Thirty-third Degree in 1925
and has served, at various times, as presiding officer of all "the Scottish
Rite Bodies." In 1928 he was Illustrious Potentate of Al Bahr Temple
of the Shrine." He was the first Master of Southern California Research Lodge.

EULOGY
CLAUDE HOWARD MORRISON

By ARTHUR PAULSEN, Past Grand Master
It was with heavy hearts that his many friends throughout the state,
and particularly those of us who worked with him at the last annual
communication of Grand Lodge. learned of the sudden and untimely
death of Most Worshipful Claude H. Morrison on November 2, 1953.
As was his custom, he had attended all the functions of Grand Lodge
and had labored long and diligently as chairman of the Finance Committee to prepare and submit its report. When that task was finished
he was greatly in need of rest and he looked forward to a period of
travel and relaxation. Immediately following the session, he and Mrs.
Morrison journeyed to Washington, D. C. where he attended the Su..
preme Council. On his way home he stopped at Detroit to take possession of a new car and then proceeded to New Orleans. Shortly after
his arrival there he was taken ill and rushed to a hospital. where he
passed away that same afternoon.
Brother Morrison was born in Pontiac, Illinois on July 10, 1887. He
received his education in the public schools of Pontiac and was gradu-

232

i33

GRAND LODGE. OP CALIFORNIA

him.self too seriously. The door of his office was always open to anyone.
No problem was too insignificant to merit his full attention, and none
too large but that he was able and willing to offer his very sound advice
regarding it. It probably is safe to say that there is scarcely any brother
who has served as Worshipful Master of his Lodge or as an Inspector
in this area during the past 30 years who has not, at one time or another,
gone to Claude Morrison for counsel and help with his problem.
"Scholarly but modest, capable but not self-seeking. basically serious but with a keen sense of humor-he was able to achieve, to a remarkable degree, that ~lance of personality" which Masonry teaches, "and
which he always exemplified as, over the years," he proceeding along
the paths of Masonry.
"He was a man among men and a Mason among Masons-a true
Grand Master among our ancient craft of builders. His richest possession was that which money can never buy-the love and respect of all
who knew him. Albert Pike once said: 'To live on in the hearts of those
we leave behind is not to die.' Of Claude Morrison, we can with all
sincerity say: 'He yet lives in all our hearts, and ever shall'."

National Bank of Los Angeles, following which he became a member
of the Board of Directors and of the Executive Trust Committee of
that bank.
Brother Gist was raised a Master Mason in Pentalpha Lodge No.
202. October 17, 1899, by Most Worshipful William Rhodes Hervey,
P. G. M. who presented to Brother Gist his 50-year Veteran's Button
in a ceremony which will long be remembered by those who were
fortunate enough to attend. Brother Gist served his Lodge as Worshipful Master in 1905, was an Inspector in 1906-1907, and then served
on various committees until his election as Junior Grand Warden in
1930, after which he became Grand Master in 1933. It was during
his term as Grand Master that Grand Lecturer Thomas J. Baker died
and under the leadership of Brother Gist our present ritualistic system
was established.
·
He was a member of Melrose Chapter 140, R. A. M.: Southern
Council 35, R. S. M.; Golden West Commandery 43, Knights Templar:
Saint Gabriel Conclave 14 of the Red Cross of Constantine: Al Malaikah Temple of the Shrine: and the Los Angeles Bodies of the Ancient
and Accepted Scottish Rite. In the Scottish Rite he received his 32nd
degree in 1907, was honored with the decoration of Knight Commander
of the Court of Honor in 1915, and was Coroneted an Inspector General
Honorary of the 33rd degree in 1919.
Closest to the heart of Brother Gist in all his Masonic service, was
the Masonic Homes of California, and for nearly 30 years he gave
outstanding ss:rvice as a member of the Board of Trustees. It was in
this work that his wide experience as a capable business man became
most evident and yet, his own great concern for the old people and for
the children, always demanded that kindliness and Christian concern
for their welfare should be the basis upon which judgments should be
made. With all his seriousness and deep concern about the affairs of
Masonry, he had a delightful sense of humor and more than once a
difficult and trying situation was relieved and resolved by a humorous
remark from Jim. If ever it could be said about a man that "he was a
Christian gentleman," James Black Gist deserved that accolade.
We have sadly missed him during the years of his illness. We shall
long continue to miss his good counsel. his leadership, and the man
himself.

EULOGY
JAMES BLACK GIST

By LLOYD E. WILSON, Past Grand Master
Among the stalwarts of this Grand Lodge for whom no designs are
drawn upon the Trestle Board because they no longer labor in the
Temple, James Black Gist stands out as a Master Craftsman. His
contribution to the cause of Freemasonry in California is more than
that of the ordinary leader because he labored in so many and varied
capacities to which he brought vast experience, great devotion, and
steadfastness to the principles and ideals of the Fraternity.
Born in Tompkinsville, Kentucky, August 8, 1868, he counted among
his ancestors in the Gist family of Maryland many distinguished leaders
of the Revolutionary War as well as of Freemasonry. He was brought
to California in 1875 and his entire life thereafter was spent in this
State in the service of his fellow citizens, particularly in the Christian
Church, of which he was an active member, and in the Masonic Lodge
which he loved so well.
Luella Hatch, to whom he was married in 1890, and his devoted
companion for more than 64 years, survives him as does their daughter,
Velma, Mrs. Elbridge R. Thrapp. A son, Charles Wooster Gist, Past
Master of Pentalpha Lodge, pre-deceased his father.
After entering upon a career of Accountancy with the Southern
Pacific Railroad, Brother Gist turned to banking and at the time of his
retirement several years ago. was Vice President of the Security First

degrees of Masonry, but actually received the three degrees in Hollywood Lodge in 1918. He served as Master of that lodge in 1925 and
was appointed Inspector for the seventy-seventh district in 1926, an
office which he held until 1936. Perhaps you will pardon the personal
element inherent in the observation that his district included Beverly
Hills Lodge, the lodge of our present Grand Master; Cahuenga Lodge,
that of the chairman of our Committee on Necrology and Liberal Arts
Lodge, my own and that each of us served as Master while Brother
Ogden was Inspector.
Our brother served this grand lodge in numerous other capacities:
the Committee on Correspondence, 1925-6; Grand Orator, 1936; Junior
Grand Warden, 1937; Senior Grand Warden, 1938; and at the communication in 1939, when for reasons of health Deputy Grand Master
Waste had to decline further office, he was elected Grand Master.
During Brother Ogden's year as Grand Master, he covered all portions of our extensive jurisdiction and faithfully discharged the duties
of his office. At the end of that year he was appointed to the Committee
on Policy and General Purposes, to the chairmanship of which committee he succeeded at our last annual communication.
Brother Ogden received the degrees of Royal Arch Masonry, Temparlism and the Scottish Rite in Los Angeles. He was decorated a
Knight Commander of the Court of Honor in 1939 and coroneted with
the Thirty-third Degree in 1945. He was also a member of the Order
of the Red Cross of Constantine and the Order of the Eastern Star.
So, in this hour, we look at the work of Brothers Morrison, Gist and
Ogden and pronounce our benediction: Well done, thou good and faithful servants. To which we add, as the haunting notes of Taps go forth:
Farewell, farewell until we meet again.

WILLIAM B. OGDEN

By ELLSWORTH MEYER, Past Grand Master
Sitting here on the platform listening to the strains from the organ,
the voice of the soloist, the report of the chairman of the committee and
the two eulogies just given of Past Grand Masters Morrison and Gist,
the truth of the statement by a late Past Grand Master that we Masons
are sentimental men has again been brought to mind. We are men of
sentiment and proud of that fact. Here in this annual memorial hour
we give proof. when we speak of the men of this grand lodge who have
demitted to the celestial lodge above during the past year.
Among those who have left our midst during the past year was
William Brayton Ogden, Grand Master during the calendar year of
1940. He was a thoroughgoing American in thought, speech and deed.
As with the two Past Grand Masters whose eulogiums we have just
heard, he came from a line of ancestors first identified with America in
very early days, although he himself was not born within the territorial
limits of the United States.
The first ancestor of our departed brother to come to the American
colonies did so in 1641. But another, of Quaker persuasion and a resident of New Jersey, removed the family domicile to Canada during the
turbulent days of the American Revolution.
It was there in Picton, in the Province of Ontario, that William
Brayton Ogden was born on August 26, 1876 in the same house in which
his father and grandfather had first seen the light of day. But his residence in Canada was of short duration, for when he was but six months
of age his family returned to the United States and took up residence in
the state of New York.
Billie, as he was known and called by all his friends, received his
education in the schools of New York; Chicago, Illinois; and Boulder,
Colorado. He was graduated from the University of Colorado with the
degree LL.B. in 1896 and began the practice of law in Boulder. Five
years later he removed to Chicago and in 1905 to Goldfield, Nevada.
It was in 1910 that he took up residence in Los Angeles and resided
there the remainder of his life.
Mrs. Ogden and he were united in marriage in 1911 and together
they have walked the pathway of life until his passing on September
twelfth.
As with our Brothers Morrison and Gist, he was singularly active
in the affairs of his church. He and his mother are credited with the
establishment of the mission which· became St. John's Parish of the
Episcopal Church in the Hollywood area and he served the parish as
vestryman and in other offices in subsequent years.
In 1903, while a resident of Chicago, he was elected to receive the

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RITUAL
-To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
FLAG CEREMONY
The Committee on Ritual reports on the resolution relative to the
Flag Ceremony which was ref erred to it for recommendation.
The resolution proposes two changes in the ceremony of Reception
of the Flag.
The flrst change is to make the movements of the deacons correspond to those in the Retirement of the Flag, namely to have the Deacons
go to the Altar with the Marshal when he retires. This change would
automatically make the same change in the Reception of Grand Lodge
Officers, since at page 58 of the Monitor it is provided that the "movements of Marshal and Deacons are same as in Flag ceremony."
The secortd change is to add what is now actually done in practice,
that is after placing the Flag in the East, or just before taking it to
retire it, the Marshal places his right hand over his heart.
The committee recommends one slight additional change in Retirement of the Flag. We recommend the adoption of the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the ceremony of Reception of the Flag (p.53 of
Monitor) .b e amended to read as follows:
After the lodge has opened, Master says: Brother Marshal, you will
retire and present the Flag of our Country.
Marshal rises, makes sign and goes to the Altar. As Marshal turns
to go to Altar, Deacons rise, take rods, and go to Altar, arriving at the
same time as Marshal. All make sign, about face and walk abreast to
the Tiler's door. Marshal opens door and goes out. Senior Deacon
takes place on north side and Junior Deacon on south side of door,
facing East. Tiler opens door for Marshal on re-entering. ( ~tc. as in
. present ceremony, to the point on page 54, where Marshal places Flag
in stand provided. Then the following: )
Marshal steps back one step, places right hand over heart for an
instant, then drops hand to side; Master puts on hat, and brethren lower
right hand to side. (Etc. to end of present ceremony).

247

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

In the retirement o( the Flag (at top of page 55) the ceremony
would read as follows:
Marshal then goes to the East, one step back from Flag, and places
~ight hand over heart. Master takes off his hat with right hand, holding
1t at left shoulder, the hand being over the heart. Brethren (except
Marshal and Deacons) stand erect and place hand over heart as Master
places hat at his shoulder. Deacons at the same time drop rod diagonally
across body to left hand without removing butt of rod from the floor and
place right hand over heart. (All except Marshal and Deacons retain
this position until Flag is passed through the door to the Tiler). Marshl
drops hand and takes Flag, goes to the Altar and stands between the
Deacons. (Etc., as in present ceremony to "Marshal closes the door")
and then the following at the end of page 55 of the Monitor. "Marshal
and Deacons return to the Altar; all break at once and return to their
places."

ORDER OF BUSINESS AT STATED MEETINGS
The Grand Master has decided that the second order of business
at Stated Meetings, under Article XII of the Uniform Code of By-Laws
(Ross Dig., sec. 133), namely, "Reports of Committees," means, and
should be construed to mean, "Reports of Investigating Committees,"
and that reports of other committees are to be made and considered
under the fifth order of business, namely, "Miscellaneous and Unfinished
Business."
The Monitor adopted by Grand Lodge has for many years followed
this interpretation of the By-laws. (See pages 46-49 of present edition
of Monitor and Officers' Manual). For many years, however, there has
existed an inconsistency in that, under the second order of business at
page 47 of the Monitor, nothing whatever is set forth except a direction
to read sections 226 et seq. of Ross Digest, while under the third order
of business, "Balloting," the Master gives the report of the investigating
committee by stating that the Committee has made a full and favorable
report, a report which should be made under the second order of business.
Investigating Committees may make three different reports, to be
acted upon by the Master or the Lodge, only one of which is followed by
a ballot. First, the committee may make an unfavorable report, if one
or more members report unfavorably. In such case "no ballot shall be
had, but the Master shall upon the reception of such report, declare the
applicant rejected." (Ross Dig., sec. 228) The proper time for reception of such report and action thereon by the Master is under this second
order of business. Second, the Committee may request that further time

Adopted.

USE OF CHARTS
Your Committee on Ritual to which was referred two resolutions,
one by the Master of Menlo Park Lodge No. 651, and one by the Master
and Wardens of Friendship Lodge No. 210, relating to use of the socalled "charts," report thereon as follows:

248

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Under Section 247 of the Ordinances, each Degree and all lectures
must be in conformity with the ritual now taught by the Grand Lecturer
and recognized by the Grand Lodge.
The present Ritual Committee has heretofore ruled that the use of
slides and other pictorial representations constitutes no part of the
Master's lectures as taught in this jurisdiction, and that no other aids
can be employed than the Monitor.
One other consideration is that if our work is to be uniform and
charts were permitted to be used, their use should be mandatory and
not optional.
The use of these so-called "charts" has however been prohibited
by the Grand Lecturer and Ritual Committee for several years, on the
further grounds that all of these charts exhibit esoteric portions of our
ritual and symbols in violation of our law. (Ross Digest, Sects. 502-504)
and constitute a violation of our obligations. We are firmly of the opinion these so-called "charts" can not be used in this jurisdiction without
changing the entire concept of secrecy of our esoteric work. .
We therefore recommend that the resolutions .be not adopted.
Adopted.

Grand Lodge."

FUNERAL CEREMONY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Ritual to which was referred two resolutions,
one by Alfred F. Baughn, a Past Master of Henry Knox Lodge No.
662, and one by Damascus Lodge No. 648, relating to the funeral service, including the use of regalia, has carefully considered these resolutions, as well as many other suggestions received from other members
of the Grand Lodge for specific changes in the funeral service, all of
which we believe should be given consideration.
While we are in favor of the amendments and changes proposed by
Brother Baughn's resolution, nevertheless any changes in the service
will involve a reprinting of the Manual, and your Committee is unanimously of the opinion that no piecemeal amendment of the funeral service should be made, hut that a very careful study and review of the
service should be made, for the purpose of embodying all changes
deemed necessary or desirable.
We therefore offer the following substitute resolution:
"RESOLVED, that the incoming Grand Master be authorized to appoint a Special Committee, or in his judgment to refer
the matter of revision of the funeral service back to the Committee
on Ritual, to make a thorough study and review of the existing
funeral service for the purpose of preparing a revision of the

REPORT OF COMMITTEE
ON RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
At our 103d Annual Communication Grand Lodge recognized The
Grand Lodge of Israel ( 1952 Proc. 301 ). Subsequent thereto on October 20, 1953, The Grand Lodge of Israel was lawfully united with the
Grand Lodge of the State of Israel under the name of the latter. So there
now exists only one regular Grand Lodge and that is the Grand Lodge
of the State of Israel. It satisfies the basic conditions of legitimacy of
origin, exclusive jurisdiction, and adherence to the ancient landmarks.
We therefore move as follows:
1. That the recognition heretofore accorded the Grand Lodge of
Israel be revoked; and
2. That the Grand Lodge of the State of Israel be recognized by the
Grand Lodge of California.
Respectfully submitted,
JOHN R. Moo RE
CHESTER H. WARLOW
ARTHUR M. WARREN
Adopted.

For more than a decade prior to 1948 California had made no con.tributions toward the Memorial Fund, resulting in a position of glaring
deficiency. which was not in keeping with the enterprising spirit of Cali.fornia. We have now redeemed this deficiency and stand at the pinacle
among other Grand Lodges. We stated in our 1953 report:
"American Freemasons have labored to create this Memorial
-this majestic temple--to the memory of the Father of our coun..
try. The great aim was not to add to the enduring luster of his
name but to hand down to coming generations a monument to
one who was an ornament to Freemasonry."
California must ever recognize and appreciate its heritage of free
men. which was hammered out by the architects of our freedom under
the leadership of the Mason, George Washington. Our Grand Lodge
should therefore accept this additional challenge. However, in light of
the undetermined direction which other Grand Lodges may take re-specting this additional challenge and in view of the financial exigencies
which now beset us, we shall not move for a continuation of the 15c
per capita levy during the current year. The $1.00 per new member will
continue as provided under our law.
I therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED:
That the funds now on hand from the 15c per capita levy and the
$1.00 per new member fund, aggregating $41.882.05, be remitted to the
George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association at or
prior to its Forty.-fifth Annual Convention on February 22, 1955, and
committed to the Endowment Fund.
Respectfully submitted,
JoHN R. MooRE
State Chairman of California

REPORT OF DIRECTORS OF MASONIC CLUB HOUSE,
LOS ANGELES

have desired, the Director and Assistant Director, Mrs. Sheldon and
Mrs. Johnson. through additional hard work have kept the Club activities
up to a relatively high level. As an example, the major dance of the year
was put on at no cost to membership dues and actually resulted in a
profit of $275.00 which was turned over to the Board of Regents for the
Muscular Dystrophy Fund at UCLA. This was a "charity" event.
Half the cost of the orchestra was contributed, as was most of the food
and other expenses. It was not only a worth while event but was a social
success and added much prestige to the Club on the campus. Similarly,
another philanthropic project was handled without cost to the membership dues. The Student Council budget this y"tar did not permit giving
the Annual Thanksgiving dinner for underprivileged children. Nevertheless the banquet was held, larger than ever, hy working up enthusiasm
among the students so that each student attending not only paid for his
own meal but sponsored one for a child. One hundred twenty five attended the banquet and it was a big success.
Low membership also caused increased problems for the Snack Bar.
It requires a minimum number of customers to pay the fixed costs. Above
that number it can operate at a profit or, as is their practice, prices are
reduced. All year it was operated on a marginal basis. However, by
operating it on a co-operative plan, it was able to provide well balanced
meals to those student members desiring such services. This is one
place where a larger membership would be a tremendous help.
The outstanding formal event of the year was, as always, the Grand
Masters Reception. This was a Dinner and Dance in honor of Grand
Master Frank Harwell, Jr. There was also a musical program furnished
by Club members.
Space of course does not permit describing all of the social adivities
but, large and small, they numbered approximately fifty during the year.
They consisted of banquets, dances, coffee hours (during orientation),
ice skating parties, bowling parties, informal parties and "open house"
events, progressive dinners, post-football dinners, Sunday suppers, etc.
Twice each year the students hold a mountain "retreat" to make plans
for the coming semester.
Since so much has been said in this report about increasing membership, we should outline what the students themselves and Mrs. Sheldon are doing to solve the problem. An attractive brochure describing
the Club and requirements for membership was sent to each incoming
student of the university. Articles about the Club appeared in the orien..
tation issue of the Daily Bruin, the school paper, received by all students.
On Orientation Day the Club maintained a booth on the campus and
distributed literature and information to inquiring students.
Traditional Open House was held on Sunday before classes started
to acquaint new stucients with the club facilities and activities. Three

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This year we are celebrating the Silver Anniversary of the Masonic
Club House on the Westwood Campus. A quarter century ago the
University of California at Los Angeles had just moved to its present
location. There were no stores or residences, but just miles of wide open
spaces. A site was selected just outside the present South Gate to the
campus and the building erected. It is still the most modern, spacious
and attractive club house in the area. Both it and the furnishings and
equipment have been kept in first class condition through money furnished by the Grand Lodge and administered by a non~profit corporation
of which we are the Board of Directors.
The Club, as distinguished from the Club House, is run by the stu..
dents themselves through their own organization and an elected Student
Council. They operate under a Constitution approved by the Board of
Directors, and are supervised by a Director and Assistant Director, Mrs.
Sheldon and. Mrs. Johnson, employed by the Board of Directors. In
addition, two members of the Board attend and take part in all Student
Council meetings. There is thus close contact with all Club activities
as well as with the physical properties under our jurisdiction.
While the Club House with all of its facilities are furnished without
charge to the students, it is essential· in order to have a well rounded
program of social activities to finance these in part through student membership dues. This is strictly a Club function and is handled through
the Student organization and Student Council. When membership is
high the dues are adequate to provide elaborate social functions which
are talked about on the campus and attract new members. When membership is low it becomes necessary to provide fewer or less elaborate
activities and thus still fewer members are attracted to the Club.
We have outlined the internal organization of our operations, which
is already too familiar to all of you who have followed our reports, in
order to add emphasis to what we reported last year with respect to the
need for encouraging greater membership. The Grand Lodge contributions cover the overhead which consists mainly of fixed charges. We
could accommodate two or three times as many students without substantially increasing the cost to Grand Lodge. The economics of the
problem are entirely different when viewed from the standpoint of the
student organization. When membership is low the dues decrease in
direct proportion, activities are cµrtailed, and there is thus the constant
danger of still lower membership. Conversely, a growing membership
tends to grow still further and makes the whole program a success.
While membership during the past year was not as high as we would

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Special Committee on Taxation has continued to function with
the same membership during the years 1953-1954.
The work of the Committee has been in large part routine advice to
subordinate lodges and the committees and other organizations operating
under the supervision of Grand Lodge.
We have had special meetings with the Masonic Homes Board 'with
reference to problems arising in that corporation.
During the year, a new internal revenue law has been enacted by
Congress but, so far, we have been unable to find any change in it with
respect to the obligations of Grand Lodge or of the subordinate lodges,
either in respect to income tax or as to reports on Social Security and
unemployment.
No change was made in the 1954 Code with respect to the status of
the ritualistic officers of the lodges, concerning which we reported in our
last year's report. Prior to 1951, ritualistic officers were excluded and
no return was required on wages paid to them. This exclusion was
eliminated in the 1951 Internal Revenue Code and it was not reinstated

260

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

by the 1954 Code. Therefore, the same advice is given that was given
last year, that no exemption can be claimed for ritualistic officers-the
organist and other ritualistic officers should be included in all returns
made, if they are paid $50.00 or more per calendar quarter.
Respectfully submitted,

R. P. WISECARVER
JAMES E. HAMMOND
ROBERT R. YoRK

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON DeMOLAY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your special committee on DeMolay, in making its annual report
would like to call to your attention an important portion of the plan
which was approved by our Grand Lodge in 1946, concerning DeMolay:
"It is a plan of education and coordination rather than one of sponsorship. Our plan would create a group of men who would act as coordinators between DeMolay and Masonry in our state. From time to
time they would be authorized to bring to our lodges the messages and
needs of DeMolay, to enlist the aid of men who would be willing to
assist in the work and to keep a watchful eye on the activities of DeMolay. Finally, they would report annually to Grand Lodge the progress of that order in California."
Your committee has followed this plan closely, yet one great need
remains, namely, the aid of individuals who are willing and capable to
serve as Chapter Dads and committee men.
Another problem faced by a number of DeMolay chapters is the
matter of flnances, caused by several factors, but is primarily due to a
greater increase in younger boys who enter the order and that of generally a smaller number of members in the individual chapter. The income
from dues and initiation fees is hardly sufficient to cover the ordinary
operating expenses of a chapter, and often there are not enough funds
to carry out a program of social and recreational activities, which are
so vital for a successful young people's organization, in addition to the
.
regular degree and chapter work.
Each committee member reports a new high, since the end of World
War II, in Programming, Membership, new chapters and general interest. Yet it is a long way from records attained dudng the 1920's.
Great interest is being shown in Northern California's new DeMolay
Camp which is being developed on the American River near Placerville,
California. Under the impetus of the East Bay group, Northern California DeMolays and Chapter committee men are constructing a beautiful camp. The cook house and several dormitories, and a bridge have
been completed, and are being used on week-ends.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

261

Visitation between DeMolay Chapters is being evidenced, one of
the most recent and successful, was the September visit of the Ukiah,
California, Chapter to the Mission Chapter in San Francisco.
Central and Southern California have shown particular interest in
the re-birth of the State DeMolay Association. This year's Conference
was held in Monterey and a larger one is planned for next year in San
Diego. Eighty-ftve Chapters are reported to have joined this new state
organization.
The San Diego County Masonic Officers Association, working in
close cooperation with the DeMolay officials of that jurisdiction and
in coordination with the Grand Lodge, DeMolay Committee man of that
area has continued to be the great example of working together for the
betterment of DeMolay and Masonry of that county.
Each year by resolution, the third week in February is set aside and
known as "DeMolay Week." That all Blue Lodges in the area are
urged to remain dark during this week. That all Masters urge their
members to attend at least one DeMolay meeting that week.
Each succeeding year since the inception in 1951 has witnessed an
increase in interest and attendance. The largest Masonic Auditorium
available in San Diego is not large enough to accommodate all those
who desired admission in 1954.
Your committee invites each Masonic Officers' Association to study
the San Diego plan. Relative to this matter, your Committee welcomes
any suggestions which will be of assistance to us in carrying out the
purpose of this committee as adopted by our Grand Lodge.
Your Com~ittee was saddened by the sudden death of Brother
Alvin E. Clark of Sacramento who had served well on this Committee
since 1951. DeMolay and Masonry will greatly miss this efficient and
fine committee man.
Brother Lester G. Bruno has been named as his successor in the
Sacramento and Northern California area.
We recommend the continuance of the Committee and that the sum
of $750.00 be appropriated to cover its necessary expenses for the ensuing year.
Respectfully submitted,

RESOLUTION RE COMMITTEE ON RECOGNITION
OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
The extension of recognition to foreign Grand Lodges is an important and essential function of our Grand Lodge. The subject should be
attended with great care to the end that complete regularity is assured
before amity is accorded. At the present no statutory authority exists
for the appointment of a Committee on Recognition of Foreign Grand
Lodges. Such appointment is at the discretion of the Grand Master
under Sec. 77 of Ross Digest.
It appears that the subject should be dignified by specific statutory
provision as proposed by Past Grand Masters John R. Moore, Chester
H. Warlow and Arthur M. Warren.
We therefore present the following:
RESOLYEO, That a new section be added to Ross Digest as follows: Sec. 78.2 A Committee on Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges,
consisting of three members, shall be appointed by the newly installed
Grand Master at each Annual Communication for a term ending at the
close of the next succeeding Annual Communication. It shall be the
duty of said Committee to investigate, consider and report with recom-

AMENDMENT OF SECTION 78
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has considered and approved the
proposal of the Committee on Lodge Financing that Section 78 of Ordinances of Grand Lodge be amended for clarification purposes to read
as follows:
"No Lodge, temple association, Lodge Trustees Committee, association, partnership or corporation, representing itself as Masonic in
character or operating for the benefit of a Masonic Lodge or Lodges,
Masonry or Masons, shall undertake any plan, scheme, project or
method whereby:
1. Real property is to be purchased, or
2. Leased for more than three years, or
3. A, Masonic temple is to be erected or altered whereby the total
expenditure will exceed the sum of $2,500.00
without first obtaining the written approval of the Committee on Lodge
Financing."
Committee on Policy and General Purposes reported concurrence.
Adopted, 5/6 vote.

ADDITION OF SECTION 78.1
Resolved: That a new section to be numbered 78.1 be added as
follows:
"All Masonic Lodges owning and operating real property and all
Masonic temple corporations operating real property and controlled by
a Masonic Lodge or Lodges, shall submit an annual profit and loss statement to the Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Financing. Such profit
and loss statement to be submitted at the close of each fl.seal year of
such Lodge or Temple Association."
Committee on Policy and General Purposes reported concurrence.
Adopted, 5/6 vote.

AMENDMENT OF SECTION 151
Resolved that Section 151 be amended to read as follows:
"A Lodge must retain the control of its own funds and property.
It may deposit its funds in a sound and reputable bank or banks. It may,
after receiving consent from the Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge
Financing, cause a corporation to be organized for the purpose of purchasing, erecting or maintaining and holding title to real estate for a

DECISION NO. 20

AMENDMENT OF SECTION 97-Sth

The Grand Master answered "NO" to the following question:
"Is conviction of a felony prior to application for Degrees,
grounds for automatic expulsion?"
The answer is correct if we eliminate the word "automatic."
An Applicant for the Degrees of Masonry must be a man of moral
conduct, coming under the tongue of good report. In 1875 this Grand
Lodge resolved that a person who had served a term in a state prison
did not come under the tongue of good report; reaffirmed in 1951.
The section in Ross Digest denominated "automatic expulsion" does
not apply to the facts in this case. Indeed, the term "automatic expulsion" is a misnomer. The section requires a trial in every case. Presentation of a certified record of conviction of a felony is prima facie evidence
only.
In this case the convicted felon should be tried for unmasonic conduct in that he concealed his record, and falsely answered the question
in his application for the Degrees as to whether he knew of any moral
reason that would prevent him from becoming a Free Mason.
Inquiry should be made in this case whether there was any unmasonic
conduct on the part of the sponsors of this man, or of members of the
investigating committee in permitting the presentation of this application
to the Lodge.
Adopted.

OLD LOS ANGELES MASON IC HALL

The Grand Master has recommended that the incoming Grand Master be authorized and directed to appoint a special committee to consider
matters relative to the proposed destruction of the first Masonic Hall
in Los Angeles, which is on North Main Street just south of the Plaza.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is of the opinion
that the members of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42 and of this Grand Lodge
would be derelict if through lack of interest or action this edifice were
demolished.
The construction of the Hollywood, Ramona and Santa Ana freeways has removed all other buildings between the hall and the freeway
and given it considerable prominence, the projected plans making the
remainder of the block, principally covered by the historic hotel, the Pico
House, an historic monument, will result in an enhancement of interest
in this hall. The area should contain this monument to Masonry as well
as the park, Plaza Church, Olvera Street and other structures.
Your Committee therefore presents the following motion and moves
'
its adoption:
appoint
"That the incoming Grand Master be authorized to
a special committee to work jointly with a committee of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42, relative to the preservation of the old Masonic Hall at 416 N. Main Street, Los Angeles; that said Grand
Master be authorized to make nominal expenditures, if necessary,
to prevent the demolition of said hall prior to our next annual
communication; that said special committee report to the Grand
Master not later than March 1, 1955, and to our next annual
communication.''
Adopted.

ATTEND ANCE OF SECRET ARIES
The Master of one of our Lodges has presented what is termed a
petition "that all Lodge Secretaries be permitted to attend or be present
at all Grand Lodge Sessions in order that they receive all necessary
information first hand and therefore be of still further value to their
respective Lodges."
In fairness to the proponent of this proposal, we should perhaps call
attention to the fact that the result he desires could not .be accomplished
by the granting of a ·petition but would require an amendment to our
Ordinance s and he has not proposed legislation to that end.
Perhaps we should also call attention to the fact that a Lodge Secretary who is pot a Past Master can attend all the sessions of the Grand
Lodge in Annual Communication except the opening ceremony and during an election, and a Secretary who is also a Past Master may be
present during those periods also.
It is a fact and not levity which prompts pointing out that no first
hand information is to be gained during the opening ceremony.
Turning to the matter of policy involved in the petition, your Committee does not believe Secretaries should be singled out and admitted
during the opening ceremonies and treasurers, deacons, stewards, mar- ·
shals, chaplains, tilers and other Master Masons excluded. No secrets
are divulged during the opening ceremonies and no valid reason exists
for the exclusion of Master Masons during the opening ceremonies and
their admission the moment those ceremonies are concluded, if seats are
available. It is probable that the beautiful opening ceremony might be
of greater interest to such brethren than some of the routine business
and their admission might tend to eliminate some of the feeling that
there is a wide chasm between the Grand Lodge and the Master Masons
who are not Lodge Officers.
If there is to be a change in policy, it should not be merely as proposed by this petition.
Because no legislation was presented and in order to put the ques-

278

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
PROCEEDINGS OF THE

tion before the house, your Committee presents the following motion
and moves its adoption:
"That the present policy of the Grand Lodge be not changed
to admit Lodge Secretaries who are not members of the Grand
Lodge during the opening ceremonies thereof or during an election therein."
Adopted.

CHARITY CONTRIBU TIONS
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes to which was referred the resolution to amend Section 158 reports as follows:
Section 158 now provides that in lieu of a floral piece for a deceased
person, the Lodge may, when requested by the family, make a contribution to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund. The resolution proposes
that under the same circumstances the contribution may be made to any
other charity selected by the family.
This Grand Lodge, at previous communications, has decided that
Lodges should not be encouraged or allowed to use Lodge funds to make
contributions to community chests, heart funds, boys' towns or other
charities. These ·decisions were sound because if the Lodge makes a contribution to one charity it immediately gets on the solicitation lists of
other charities and, as you brethren know, it is difficult to say "no" to
one charity when they remind you that you have helped another or a
competing charity. The fact that the contribution was made in lieu of
flowers does not show on the solicitation list and the minute the Lodge
makes a contribution it is going to be besieged with requests for other
contributions. The door is open and will be pushed wider.
There is another reason for our recommendation on this resolution.
Masonry, and that means your Lodge and you brethren, are supporting
two fine charities, the two Masonic Homes, plus Boards of Relief for
sojourning Masons, plus Employment Services, plus helping your needy
brethren. We are in the nature of a charitable institution. Charities do
not contribute to each other.
Brethren, if Bowers are not desired by the family, a letter of sympathy is much more appreciated and more personal than any contribution
to another charity, and it doesn't bring down upon your heads dozens of
requests for donations. You have wisely kept this door closed and we
recommend that you continue to keep it closed. We recommend a "no"
vote on this resolution.
A motion to adopt the original resolution was defeated.

LIABILITY INSURANC E
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was
referred the recommendations of the Special Committee on Insurance,
reports as follows:
The report presents a serious problem which might become tragic

279

today, tomorrow or anytime. Approximately 214 Lodges do not have any
protection against damage suits based on persons being injured in the
premises they occupy or by reason of negligence of their representatives.
The members of these 214 Lodges are without any protection from such
suits and might be bankrupted at any time.
Let me illustrate what I mean. Suppose someone attending one of
these Lodges fell downstairs because of a faulty carpet, a worn step or
some similar reason and broke an arm or a leg. That person might sue
the Lodge and every member in it and collect any judgment from the
Lodge or any or all of the members of that Lodge.
Suppose the Master of the Lodge was driving his car on Lodge business and ran into someone. That person might sue the Lodge and every
member of that Lodge and collect damages from the Lodge or any or
all of the members of that Lodge.
That would be tragic and could very well bankrupt that Lodge and
every member of it and yet these 214 Lodges have no liability insurance
to protect themselves or their members. Why? I don't know. This
protection could be secured for only a few cents per member each year.
There is the problem and its possible tragic result of no insurance.
What is the answer?
The Special Committee on Insurance has suggested two alternatives.
One is to have Grand Lodge secure a blanket policy to cover Grand
Lodge and all constituent Lodges and pay the cost. Your Committee
does not approve this proposal because approximately 159 Lodges carry
their own insurance with local people, or through their members, and
want to conti:g,ue to do so. They are not part of the problem.
The other proposal is that all constituent Lodges be required to
carry the same broad coverage and amounts of insurance as Grand
Lodge carries, furnish evidence of such insurance to the Grand Secretary or be covered by insurance secured by Grand Lodge and cost thereof
charged to the Lodge.
Your Committee does not believe the Lodges should be required to
carry the same amount of insurance that Grand Lodge carries, because
the Lodges may not all need this extensive coverage, but we do believe
that all Lodges should carry liability insurance because, as I have stated,
if they do not they are inviting bankruptcy for themselves and their
members. No Lodge should place itself or its members in this position.
Your Committee accordingly makes the following recommendations:
1. That all constituent Lodges be required to carry adequate liability
insurance and furnish evidence of such insurance to the Grand Secretary
before December first of each year. If such evidence of insurance is not
received ·before December 1st, then the Grand Secretary shall have the
authority to purchase adequate liability insurance for the account of the
constituent Lodge and collect the premium from such Lodge.
2. That this subject ·he made a part of the discussions at District

280

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Officers Meetings and Inspectors Conferences each year to acquaint
the officers of Lodges and inspectors with the liabilities involved and
the necessity for adequate coverage.
Brethren, Grand Lodge has for many years tried to bring this problem to the attention of Lodges and Lodge Officers but we still have
approximately 214 Lodges who have done nothing about it. We cannot,
in good conscience, allow the members of these Lodges to be left .open
to this liability. It could be tragic yet it can be taken care of for a few
cents per member.
We move the adoption of this resolution.
Adopted.

DE MOLAY SPONSORSIBP

The following resolution, proposed by Brother John Raatz, Senior
Warden of San Gorgonio Lodge No. 668, has been submitted to your
Committee on Policy and General Purposes for recommendation:
"Whereas, the present ordinances of the Grand Lodge of California
prevent constituent Lodges from giving direct aid to De Molay Chapters, and
Whereas the De Molay Chapter in Banning is now without a sponsor and has no prospect of acquiring one, and
Whereas, other Grand Lodges such as Massachusetts do permit
such aid,
Now, therefore, be it resolved that the Grand Lodge of California
adopt a resolution to permit constituent Lodges to sponsor such De
Molay Chapters."
Your Committee finds itself in a position identical to that of an
earlier Committee on Policy and General Purposes which, in 1924 (See
Section 521 of Ordinances), reported that despite an entire accord and
sympathy with the ideals, aims, and purposes of the Order of De Molay,
the Committee did not "Feel that this Grand Body should take over the
responsibility for the movement, splendid and helpful as it is."
Grand Master Crites, in 1924, voiced the policy which has governed
our attitude in this respect since that time, when he reminded the Grand
Lodge that the "De Molay organization is not an adjunct of Masonry
nor a recruiting ground for Masonry."
Your Committee considers it not at all unlikely that authorized sponsorship of De Molay Chapters would soon lead to embarrassing demands
for similar sponsorship of Bethels of Job's Daughters and other organizations claiming alliance with Masonry, responsibility for which this Grand
Lodge cannot accept.
Your Committee, therefore, feels that it must concur in the findings
of the predecessor Committee: and recommends that, despite a temporary adverse effect upon the Banning Chapter, the sponsorship of any
De Molay Chapter by a Lodge of this Jurisdiction be not approved, and
that the proposed resolution be rejected.
A motion to adopt the original resolution was defeated.

PER CAPITA TAX LIMITATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Past Masters Christianson, Fitkin, McAdams, MacKellar, Page, and
Kincaid of Santa Barbara Lodge No. 192 having submitted the following
resolution:
"That the necessary legislation be enacted whereby the Per
Capita Tax assessed the constituent Lodges by the Grand Lodge,
shall not exceed 203 (twenty percent) of the minimum dues established by the Grand Lodge,"
and such resolution having been referred by the Grand Master to your
Committee on Policy and General Purposes,
Your Committee reports as follows:
1. Reference to Sec. 251 of the Ordinances discloses that the present
assessment, established by this Grand Lodge during previous Communications as a minimum requirement for effective operation, is in excess
of the proposed 203 limitation.
2. Your Committee considers that legislation establishing a speciBed
limit upon the aforesaid Per Capita Tax will result in unnecessary and
undesirable inflexibility by virtue of the provisions of Sec. 350 of the
Ordinances, namely, that a 5/6th vote of the members present at any
future Communication would be required to effect any necessary adjustment of the tax.
3. Your Committee feels that the members of the Grand Lodge, at
the annual Communications, should remain free, as they are at present,
to adjust the per capita assessment upon constituent Lodges in accordance with the current requirement, unhampered by any inflexible limiting
Ordinance.
For these reasons, your Committee recommends that the proposed
resolution be not adopted.
Past Grand Master Lawlor's point of order that "the resolution is
out of order" was sustained by the Grand Master.

certain charitable Foundation or Foundations wherein the principal purpose of which, among others, shall be the owning and
operating of Masonic Temples for the use of such Grand Lodge,
and that all surplus funds from the operation thereof by such
Foundation or Foundations shall be, from time to time, disbursed
and/or donated to the Masonic Homes of California, a non-profit
California corporation."
In the opinion of your Committee, it would be extremely unwise to
allow the Grand Lodge to become a party to a so-called tax savings device for the benefit of unnamed Masonic Temples.
The subject of so...called Charitable Foundations is continually being
screened and scrutinized by the various tax authorities of the State and
of the Nation. Any participation on our part in such a move could very
likely endanger the present satisfactory tax structure which our Masonic
Homes Corporation enjoys.
The Masonic Homes and its Endowment Fund have long been considered in a favorable light by the various tax agencies and any move
which might limit or destroy such a benefit should be looked upon with
disfavor.
We, therefore, recommend a "NO" vote on the resolution.
A motion to adopt the original resolution was defeated.

HAWAIIAN VISITATION
Past Grand Master Leslie Wood reported for the Committee on
Policy relative 'to the recommendation of the Grand Master that Past
Grand Master Wood make a trip to the Hawaiian Islands. Brother
Wood moved that the Grand Master's recommendation be not adopted,
and the vote being taken the recommendation of the Committee was
not adopted.
The question being raised as to just what the situation was after the
Report of the Committee on Policy relative to the Hawaiian Islands had
been rejected, and to clarify the matter, the Deputy Grand Master asked
those who wished Past Grand Master Wood to go to the Islands to
vote "yes" and those opposed to vote "no."
The affirmative vote prevailed.

PROCEDURE FOR MEMORIAL TEMPLE ERECTION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The following resolution has been submitted to the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes:
·
1. "That no work be commenced on the California Memorial Temple
until sufficient.money 'to erect, complete, furnish and equip said Temple
in its entirety to the end such Temple may be dedicated unencumbered."
2. "That neither the credit of this Grand Lodge nor any of its agencies be pledged directly or indirectly, nor shall any of its securities or
property owned by it or any of its agencies be used as security or collateral in the borrowing of any money for the purpose of erecting, furnishing or equipping said Temple without prior approval of this Grand
Lodge at an Annual Communication called for by that purpose."
Your Committee r~ports as follows:
I. The Grand Lodge in 1953 approved longe term financing as part
of the building program.
2. The Grand Lodge has provided ample safeguards against any
unsound financing in required approval by the Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master, the Senior Grand Warden, the Junior Grand Warden,
the Grand Treasurer, the Grand Secretary, the Chairman of the Committee on Finance, and the Chairman of the Committee on Lodge Financing of any financing plan.
3. That the above Committee should not be hampered by restriction
as set forth in this resolution.

(rejected).
